subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR SPONSORED IMMIGRANTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, whereas those who sponsored immigrants prior to 1967 remain responsible for the immigrants for life, and whereas those who sponsored family members between 1967 and 1978 remain responsible for them for life, and whereas those sponsored after 1978 remain the responsibility of their sponsor for ten years, it is obvious that a great discrepancy has been created for new Canadians and their sponsors prior to 1978 who are not being treated equally before the law. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski):
That the government give immediate consideration to making the ten-year responsibility period retroactive for all immigrants sponsored prior to 1978.

In contrast, the government of Ontario has followed the sterling example set by the Clark government and speedily called the byelection in York South, an opposition-held riding. That the House demand that the Prime Minister today follow the example set by the Clark and Davis governments and announce dates for byelections in Timiskaming, Leeds-Grenville, and Broadview-Greenwood. subsubtopic: POLAND-CALL FOR RELEASE OF SOLIDARITY LEADER, LECH WALESA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Lech Walesa has been held in internment since the military takeover in Poland last December when martial law was proclaimed and the Solidarity movement suspended. About 3,000 Poles demonstrated peacefully in Poznan on the anniversary of the 1956 disturbances, requesting his release and thereby showing that Solidarity in Poland is still alive. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Mac-Bain) and the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That in the interest of the greater peace and security of Poland, this House urge the Polish authorities to release and restore freedom of movement to Solidarity leader, Lech Walesa.

subsubtopic: MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. During the last election the Prime Minister promised to keep the growth of government spending to less than the growth rate of the Gross National Product. The Prime Minister broke this promise when his first budget increased government spending by 24 per cent. The Prime Minister again broke his promise this year when government spending increased 20 per cent, for a two-year staggering total of 44 per cent, twice the rate of increase of the Gross National Product. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Okanagan-Similk-ameen (Mr. King):
That this House demand the Prime Minister stop the flim-flam and start acting with reason, with responsibility, and even with sanity, and immediately reduce this uncontrolled spending growth to an increase of 6 per cent as he is asking the poor and elderly of this country to do.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: RESPONSIBILITY FOR SPONSORED IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question which obviously relates to a case which has
come to light recently in the Toronto area, regarding an application for welfare under provincial rules. I would point out to the House, first of all, that eligibility for welfare is a provincial decision and has very little to do with any decision being made under the federal jurisdiction. It is within provincial rights and responsibilities.
The Immigration Act provides that sponsorship is very much a moral obligation for those who have undertaken to sponsor a relative. In effect, it is a special privilege to come into this country under relaxed criteria, but sponsor responsibility is not legally enforceable under the old act. It is enforceable under the 1978 act. A judgment has to be made by the municipality as to whether it will consider the provisions of the 1978 act as part of the criterion for eligibility.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the provincial governments and municipalities are hanging their decisions in this particular case and, I understand, in other cases, on the agreement that was signed by the sponsors pre-1967 and pre-1978. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am indicating that the whole question of the enforcement of the sponsorship provisions is only legally enforceable under the provisions of the 1978 Immigration Act. We are saying to the municipalities that in this case their judgment on who is eligible for welfare benefits should be based upon the usual criteria applied. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak to a subject as important as this budget. As everyone in this House is aware, for several years, and especially during the last year or year and a half, industrialized countries have been faced with very serious problems. What happened to our economy, which had been doing so well in the years from 1970 to 1974? Well, we all know that around 1973 or 1974, oil prices increased by an incredible 700 or 800 per cent. Inevitably, the increased price of oil was reflected in production and transportation costs, and oil consuming countries have all had to raise their prices tremendously in order to continue to make a profit or just to break even. With the oil crisis came inflation, which started in 1974-75 at between 6 and 7 per cent and now, in 1982, in Canada, has risen to nearly 12 per cent. Because of inflation, in every collective agreement negotiated subsequently, employees have demanded wage increases at least equivalent to the rate of inflation, in other words, between 8 and 12 per cent. Producers had to pass on these increases in the prices for their products and we have been in this inflationary spiral for a number of years, which is one of the reasons we are now in a recession.
Furthermore, a few months ago the powerful United States decided to raise interest rates to previously unheard-of levels, namely 18, 19 and even 20 per cent. The reason: the U.S. wants to bring back petro-dollars invested throughout the world. Petro-dollars are invested in Canada and also in France, Great Britain and Italy, and it is a fact that people with money to invest, whether it is $100,000, $10,000 or $10 million, are going to invest it in countries where they can get the best return on their investment. In this case, they are taking their money to the United States which is paying the highest rates in the world. That is why millions of dollars have been pouring in to the United States. Here in Canada, if we do not want our economy to be bled dry for the benefit of the U.S., like many other countries we must raise our interest rates to compete with U.S. rates.
One often wonders why the United States is trying to bring home all those petro-dollars. I am not sure about the reasons, but I do have a question. As we all know, a number of European countries, including Germany and France, are negotiating with the U.S.S.R. for the construction of a pipeline from Siberia to Europe, which will carry Siberian natural gas to energy-hungry Europeans. Obviously, the United States is not very happy about this, because in the event of a serious conflict between the U.S.S.R. and our countries, the first thing the
U.S.S.R. will do is cut off the supply of natural gas to our allies, namely Germany, Italy, France and Great Britain. Is this why the U.S. wants to repatriate its petro dollars, to prevent the financing of a megaproject that is going to cost several billion dollars? I am not sure but it might be one of the reasons. What I do know, however, is that in the short term, the U.S. economy will certainly benefit from the situation, because with all this money, the Americans will be able to build a lot of factories, and subsequently provide jobs for their people. Even if in the U.S. unemployment is also running at about 10 per cent, an increase in the number of jobs may be expected in the short term. I am not so sure about the longterm effects, however, because the U.S. dollar is already worth 25 or 28 per cent more than the Canadian dollar, and European currencies have fallen about 50 per cent, in terms of the American dollar, from where they were about two years ago. This means that as time goes on, the U.S. will find it increasingly difficult to export its products and, conversely, other countries will find it much easier to export their goods to the U.S. Nevertheless, I am not too worried about the U.S. I am sure they realize what is involved, and they had reasons for taking the action they did.
Where does Canada stand in these difficult times of very high interest rates? As 1 said earlier, we have almost matched U.S. rates, while our Canadian dollar has fallen. Today, our dollar is worth about 78 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar, which does not look too good. However, if we compare the performance of our Canadian government with that of all other industrialized countries, including economically strong countries such as France, Germany and Japan, we realize that our dollar is very strong, because although it is worth 78 cents in U.S. terms, currencies in European countries have fallen by 50 per cent compared with the American dollar. And if we draw a comparison with the Canadian dollar, two years ago, one franc was worth 28 or 29 cents, while today, in 1982, although our dollar is down to 78 cents in U.S. terms, one French franc is worth only 17 or 18 cents in Canadian money. So we can say that Canada's policies have still been quite satisfactory, and that today, although our dollar may be weaker than the American dollar, it is much stronger than the currencies of all other industrialized countries.
People tell us that paying 18 per cent interest is outrageous, and I agree. If here in Canada we wanted to have a 12 per cent rate, while U.S. rates are as high as 18 per cent, on the face of it, it might make things easier for our industries, but we all know that investors in Canada would transfer their Canadian funds to the United States, and there would be no capital left in Canada to finance our Canadian industries. In fact, the initial improvement would be followed in a few months by a definite worsening of the situation. It would not be impossible

July 8, 1982

to reduce interest rates, but if we were to do so, we would have to prevent an outflow of Canadian capital toward the United States and other countries. The procedure to be followed in this regard would be the adoption of an exchange control law. With such legislation Canadians could not take money out of Canada to invest it in other countries at their will. I must admit that, in the short term, this could solve the problem for a few months. However, we know quite well that, in Canada, we not only need money from Canadians, but also, from foreigners in order to develop our country, whether it be the tar sands projects which are now facing problems, the James Bay project, which has cost us $18 billion, or other major Canadian projects. If we did implement exchange controls, no foreign company would be interested in investing in Canada since it could not get back the profits to its own country, and the situation would be even worse.
Compared with what is happening in the United States, our economy is at a standstill. In addition to interest rates, there are certainly several reasons for our economic ills. I do not want to describe them all today, because some of them are obvious, others are apparent and others are more subtle. However, I would like to mention a few of them because I believe that we, the elected representatives of the people, on all sides of the House, have a duty to make suggestions so that all Canadians may discuss them and gain the best possible understanding of the problems. One important problem is the fact that wages have increased more quickly in Canada than in the United States, which means that our production costs are often higher than in the United States. This is a problem, but it is not the worst one because I agree that Canadian workers should earn a good living. However, Canada is dangerously and obviously lagging behind in the area of productivity. If we compare Canadian and American productivity, we find that ours is about 20 per cent lower. Who is responsible? The various government levels are partially responsible. Because of their abusive wage demands and working conditions, labour unions heavily share that responsibility. Consequently, the workers who make up the membership of these unions are also responsible. I would like to give a few examples. In Quebec, for instance-and I suppose that the situation is similar in many Canadian provinces-if you are a carpenter working on construction sites, you have a certain territory where you can work, let us say the area of Montreal. If your contractor accepts a building contract in Trois-Rivieres, for each employee he hires in Montreal to work in Trois-Rivieres, he will have to hire a certain number of local workers. This means that if a Montreal contractor needs 100 employees for a job in Trois-Rivieres and hires 50 employees in the Montreal area, he will have to hire 50 workers in the Trois-Rivieres region. As everyone must realize, the best workers from these regions already have a job because the best workers in any field can always find a job. This contractor will therefore have to hire workers who are not as good, and therefore not as productive. When he makes his submission, he takes this fact into account
The Budget-Mr. Demers
and increases his prices by 10, 15 or 20 per cent to compensate for a lower productivity.
We are now going through a public transport strike in Montreal. Those who sell tickets have been asked to give change to the public. This is part of their job, they must collect the money and give change to the public. They believe that this is not their job, that they do not have to do the work, and they are even talking about going on strike. This would not give them any more money, but they are putting obstacles in the way. I went to the hospital very recently because my youngest son had an operation, and I witnessed something which surprised me. A nurse dropped a bottle on the terrazzo floor. Two and three-year-old toddlers were playing around the glass. The nurse had no right to pick up the shattered glass, she must make a call because the union says a cleaning attendant must pick up the glass. So, according to union instructions, the nurse called the cleaning attendants. Fifteen minutes later, for some reason, the glass was still on the floor, with the children around. I took a sheet of paper and picked up the glass; because I am not unionized, nobody can stop me from doing it. Such situations are utterly stupid. First of all, children could have been harmed, and this is very important; second, the nurse could have picked up all the glass in two minutes. Just imagine! She called somebody that started from the other end of the building, who may have walked half an hour or fifteen minutes to get there, then he took five or ten minutes to pick up the glass and had to walk another quarter of an hour to get back to work.
It is because of such nonsense that no salary increases are granted, but productivitywise, each one of us Canadians has to pay for these mistakes with our taxes. In that context, I feel that we Canadians all have to start thinking, because we must understand that today we are in competition with the United States, Japan and every other nation. If we are to protect our jobs, we will not do so by asking Canadians to put in terrific hours, to work on the double, but simply by requesting that within those eight or seven and a half hours people work, they give a full day's work, and I am convinced that with the level of education in Canada and our mining potential, this country can make for very pleasant living and can compete very easily with any other nation.
Workers are not the only ones at fault. Our businessmen also share the responsibility. Quite recently the Canadian government had to guarantee several million dollars to Chrysler because that corporation was in serious difficulty. We guaranteed several million dollars to protect those jobs. But how come that since 1973, since the oil crisis, when we all realized that automobiles should be smaller, the Chrysler Corporation kept on producing cars that were exceedingly large, exceedingly heavy, and that guzzled a lot of gas? Consumers, of course, were aware of this and sales went down. Therefore, that corporation was clearly at fault. I could refer

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Demers
to other cases, of which there are several. This points to the responsibility of management, especially in the case of large corporations and, amazingly, in the case of that corporation.
1 mentioned earlier that governments have a goal, the federal government, provincial governments, municipal governments. We have so many regulations and paperwork that we require businessmen and employees to spend part of their working hours completing forms, complying with regulations and all kinds of things. This is hindering productivity. We, as government, realized this and, some time ago we set up a committee to look into all these demands on industry, with a view to reducing them as much as possible. An industry that must use 5 per cent of its time completing forms has a 5 per cent productivity loss. As I said, all governments are guilty to some extent. These include provincial governments, and I should like to state a few facts which affect me most as a Quebecer. Our province of Quebec is making mistakes, tremendous mistakes. Very recently, it bought the Asbestos Corporation. Everybody has been aware for several years that asbestos will face great difficulties in the future, that asbestos will become difficult to sell, that it has been banned in several countries because some studies have demonstrated a direct link between its use and cancer. Sales have been going down for several years. Yet, the Quebec government stuck to its idea of spending several millions of Quebecers' money to purchase this corporation. Now, it has bought it, paying top dollar for it, and the directors of this corporation, who in my opinion are very clever businessmen, played their cards extremely well. They behaved as though they did not want to sell to push the price upward, as though they felt very badly about it. But 1 suggest that, when they sold their company, they were the happiest directors in the world. As a matter of fact, Quebec has had to lay off several hundreds of its asbestos workers. Quebec is the new owner of the corporation, but its workers are no longer working, something which had been foreseen! Quebec residents pay between 20 and 25 per cent more income tax than their Ontario counterparts because of mistakes such as this one and because of a lack of restraint in their economy. The Quebec government has just bought, as I said, the Asbestos corporation, just as it had bought the Sidbec steel plant a few years previously, the Sidbec steel plant which is accumulating millions of dollars in deficits every year; now, it is anxious to get rid of it, even at a loss. It would have been better advised not to buy Asbestos and to keep the Sidbec steel plant.
If you compare the budget of Quebec with that of Ontario, you can come up with interesting findings. In 1974-75, Quebec spent $7.9 billion and Ontario $9.6 billion. Ontario clearly spent more than Quebec, but Ontario has a population of approximately 9 million and Quebec 6 million. In 1980-81, Quebec spent $19 billion and Ontario $17 billion. If there are some of you who could explain to me how Quebec with a population of 6 million could spend $19 billion, while Ontario with a population of 9 million managed to spend only $17
billion, that is, less than Quebec with 9 million population I would be pleased to hear them!
Comparing totals is always difficult. But if you determine the spending on an individual basis, you will find that in 198081, the per capita spending in Quebec was $3,018, and when I say on an individual basis, I include pensioners, children, handicapped people, everybody who is not working. The per capita spending in Ontario was $2,071. Quebec, therefore, for every person living on its territory spent $947 more than Ontario did for its own people, while it spent only $109 more in 1974-75. An increase of 900 per cent over six or seven years. If this keeps up, Quebec residents, needless to say, will continue to pay more taxes than their Ontario counterparts, not only during this generation, but during many generations to come.
To continue in the same vein, I would point out that since the present government came to power in the province of Quebec, civil servants have been hired by the ton. A slew of new departments were set up to accommodate friends of the party and, naturally, the bill is now being paid which makes things pretty rough. Now, to come back to the over-all situation in Canada, Canadians lack certain things, of course; but despite our weaknesses, and we must speak of them too-it is a good thing to speak of them-we must not become overly pessimistic. Canada and Canadians should feel confident that we will soon have worked our way out of this crisis.
Still, the fact is that when we compare the potential of Canada with that of other countries, we realize that all in all we are privileged. Canada is a country where the level of education is just about the highest in the whole world, and therefore where science and technology are also extremely advanced. We are lucky, not because we are Canadians, but because we have been lucky! We live in a country where there is an abundance of oil, part of which is in oil sands and hence very costly to extract; but it is still there. It gives us a measure of security, and considering those countries which have none at all, that is an asset. In addition to oil, we all know we have natural resources such as forests, water, both salt and fresh, iron, zinc in fantastic quantities. In light of those factors, we can look to a very promising future and as Canadians, we should stop being pessimistic and look to the future with confidence. Indeed, the last budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) demonstrated vividly that the country is now going through difficult times over the short term and that steps must be taken to help our industry.
This year of course, we know that the inflation rate in Canada will reach 11.8 per cent while south of the border it will be 6 or 7 per cent. We can easily understand that if those conditions were allowed to prevail for two or three years, we would no longer be competitive. Canada must therefore bring its inflation rate down so that it is roughly the same as that in the United States. Accordingly, the matter which came under
July 8, 1982

consideration was not a salary freeze, but a 6 per cent reduction in the forthcoming year and a 5 per cent reduction the year after, which would contribute to reducing our own inflation rate to a level comparable to the American one. And why are the United States so important? They are impotant because 75 per cent of our national trade is done with the Americans. Our companies are experiencing difficulties and this is understandable when we have to pay 18, 19 per cent interest rates. It is quite difficult for those companies to make profits and quite often they incur losses which are serious enough to bring them to the verge of bankruptcy.
Well, the government and the Minister of Finance have decided that the federal government would pay 4 per cent of those interest rates to reduce them by 4 points and this will first of all help the construction industry. The construction industry is the most Canadian of all industries because all its employees are necessarily Canadians. All building materials are manufactured in Canada whether it is lumber, gyproc, asphalt shingles, cement, electric wire, or plumbing equipment. This economic sector is entirely Canadian and I think it is the first one which should be assisted. Well, buyers of new homes will be eligible for a $3,000 grant, but they actually will get more than $3,000, because $3,000 is not a very high amount compared with the prices of houses today. What is more significant is the fact that the mortgage rates on houses will be reduced by 4 per cent and this is a lot, because it means 4 per cent this year, next year, the following year and every year as long as the same individual remains the mortgagor of his house.
We know quite well that in the near future, maybe in an unforseeable but near future, the interest rates should stabilize and become much more normal. To a prospective buyer of a new house concerned about economic restrictions, we say: You will pay 4 per cent less interest than the normal rate throughout the period when it will remain high and we know that to own a home has been for several years the best investment that can still be made in Canada.
I think that those measures will stimulate the construction industry and help Canadians become home owners. We will also help all small and medium-size businesses by reducing their interest rates by 4 per cent. Of course that will make a big hole in the Canadian budget. The deficit had to be increased to meet those requirements. But there is one thing to be said, namely that a government is administered exactly the opposite of the way a family budget is administered. In a crisis when everything is going very badly, a government must spend more to help create jobs and to help businesses invest, expand and hire people. With the creation of those jobs, there will be lots of work in two or three years and practically all the unemployed will have found work. By then the government will collect many taxes from the labour force and from businesses that will be making profits, so we should do the contrary
The Budget-Mr. Yurko
and pull in the purse strings because full employment often fuels inflation. I said it was exactly the opposite of a family budget because a family has to tighten its belt when things go badly and it must immediately act with caution. But the government must spend money for a specific purpose, and that is to create jobs for Canadian workers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to participate in this debate. I wish first to speak briefly about the domestic economic climate and perhaps, if I have not been too windy, to touch on the international economic situation if time permits. I do not wish to abuse the privileges of the House, so I will try to limit my remarks to less than 20 minutes.
Canada today is in the midst of cost-push inflation, sustained primarily by high cost money, the high cost of governments and the very high costs of overhead, management salaries and skilled labour in the private sector.
Our nation is living beyond its means and adjustments are desperately needed. The brutal force of inflation is the result of living beyond our means. The nation has two choices: to continue to live beyond its means and thereby live on debt and an accelerating cycle of inflation, eventually resulting in the short-term collapse of the economic cycle, or by self-imposed restraint and Draconian government measures to lower temporarily the expectations of all Canadians, cut the inflationary cycle and then follow with a cycle of confidence and growth.
It is easy to heap the blame upon the federal government or a successive number of governments for the economic disaster facing Canadians today. Although the federal government must shoulder much of the blame, it is not the only culprit. All present provincial governments are living on debt, meeting their obligations with borrowings, as are most Canadians. All governments in Canada, regardless of political persuasion,

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Yurko
have simply become too big, not necessarily in the economic planning sector but certainly in the administration of a massive variety of programs which people often could and would much rather do for themselves.
All governments in Canada are taxing away for redistribution some 45 per cent of the gross national product of this nation, and this figure is going up. The federal government accounts for one-third and the provinces and municipalities the other two-thirds.
All governments are redistributing borrowed wealth. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) told us in his recent budget, the federal government deficit in this fiscal year will be $19.6 billion. The budgetary deficits of all the provinces together this fiscal year are projected to be $9.4 billion. I suspect that the actual figure will be more like $12 billion.
At the end of the current fiscal year, the debt structure of the federal government will reach about $145 billion and that of the provinces about $70 billion. This is a debt load of about $9,000 for every woman, man and child in Canada. With interest rates in the region of 20 per cent, this is just too much for the Canadian people and the Canadian economy to sustain for too long. Therefore, the first order of a federal budget and indeed every provincial budget is fiscal restraint. Governments simply must restrain themselves. The alternative is economic collapse and chaos and a long drawn out cycle of recovery. It is the next 12 to 24 months that are critical. Some of us have seen clearly this economic scenario that was developing over the last several years and indeed the last several months.
During the last few months I have tried to be constructive. I introduced a series of motions and made several speeches in this House with regard to needed economic policies and strategies. Permit me, Mr. Speaker, just to review a few of the motions 1 introduced under Standing Order 43. On May 6 I moved a motion stating that I felt certain that the Minister of Finance may wish to second it, and the Speaker actually put the motion. At that time I said:
Madam Speaker, the federal government's fiscal and economic policy cannot expect solely the private sector to cure the inflationary ills of the nation. The public sector must bear its share of the burden as it takes some 45 per cent of the GNP with little or no positive influence on productivity. Therefore I move:
That the government immediately adjust its economic strategy to:
(1)	allow the dollar to drop by at least 5 per cent of its value and then maintain a new level through the appropriate fiscal and monetary policy;
(2)	immediately call a federal, provincial and municipal conference to stabilize for at least two years the salaries and benefits of all public servants whose income is greater than $25,000 per year;
(3)	cut government expenses in a Draconian fashion and introduce a new budget incorporating the necessary incentives for growth;
(4)	restructure the National Energy Program immediately;
(5)	undertake with the provinces a massive public works program on a national basis to create jobs.
I moved that motion on May 6. It is interesting that the dollar since then has dropped by 5 per cent, wages in the public sector are being stabilized for two years, a new budget has been introduced, the National Energy Program has been significantly and beneficially changed and construction programs are being undertaken.
On February 17 I gave a speech in this House asking for selective stimulation of the housing industry for job creation. In the same speech, I asked "that a task force be put together at the earliest opportunity to come forth with a whole series of programs by governments for selectively stimulating the Canadian economy and creating jobs without necessarily increasing inflation". All of this is being done in the new budget. I was certainly pleased to hear HUDAC's recent response to the stimulative housing initiatives in the budget.
On May 11 and again on May 20, I moved a motion "that all Members of Parliament voluntarily accept a 10 per cent cut in their basic salaries", to show leadership in this House and to the nation. I followed these motions by a private members' bill to limit MP's increases to a maximum of 6 per cent. Some opposition members accused me of grandstanding and all sorts of insincere motives. Well, this budget has both an MP salary reduction and a limitation on increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the next two years. I have heard no one scream against these budgetary provisions.
Again on June 9 I introduced a motion. I stated:
-equity investment pessimism is pervasive in Canada. Canadians are investing their money outside Canada and in high-interest-bearing bonds and certificates. This has substantively curtailed the ability to generate equity capital in Canada and has jeopardized the survival of small business in Canada because of the high cost of debt capital. A new budget is necessary to create confidence in the Canadian economy, and it must contain incentives for equity investment. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That any new budget abolish capital gains taxation on all equity investment
in Canadian registered companies.
We recognized, as so many of us have, the massive transfer of equity capital to debt capital in the nation, also imported capital. Effectively, the Minister of Finance has basically introduced such measures in the budget. He proposed indexing the gains to inflation for equity investment in Canadian owned companies, but he might just as well have gone the full mile and totally removed capital gains on investments in Canadian companies. He increased the amount of paperwork which is becoming extensive in the area of capital gains taxation.
I am asked what is my position on the June 28 budget. First, let me say that it was desperately needed. Second, its intent and purpose is short term. It cannot be otherwise in this very turbulent economic cycle. Third, its goals are to cut inflation, hopefully to 6 per cent in two years, bottom out the recession cycle, sustain a short-term economic holding action and, finally, initiate the beginning of a new and dynamic growth cycle, and to do this without massive and sweeping government legislative action across the entire society. Voluntary restraint is still partially our choice. The government has finally whipped up enough courage to provide some desperately needed economic leadership to the nation.
It is my intention to support the restraint measures embodied in Bill C-124 and vote for the principles in that bill. Rounded out, the budget has three basic elements. First, public sector restraint; second, investment stimulation through equity
July 8, 1982

incentive financing and lower debt financing; third, job creation through a variety of fiscal juggling. In the first element, the budget goes as far as the government dare go on wage restraints, but this must surely be looked upon only as the beginning of public sector restraint, both at the federal and provincial levels. Surely it must be followed by employment reduction through early retirement, as the Imperial Oil Company did so adequately in the last few days, and a reduction in the unproductive expenditures in all areas of government.
In the second element, which is investment stimulation, the government could have gone even further, although I expect that the special advisors committee will be pushing like hell.
In my estimation, the third element of job-creation is marginal and much help is needed from the provinces in this area. I hope that the government will continue discussions with the provinces to initiate an increasing variety of job-creation programs, particularly in the construction industry.
I know that it is easy, as has been done by many, to say that the budget measures are not enough that some elements are inequitable, that some elements are missing, that the emphasis is misplaced and that it may be tricky or deceptive. 1 listened to the speeches of the leaders of the two opposition parties with mixed emotions. I was particularly impressed with some of the thoughts of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). Much wailing and gnashing of teeth was directed toward the government's over-enthusiasm at fiscal restraint in some areas, particularly in areas like reducing the indexing of old age pensions to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the next two years. On Canada Day, or Dominion Day, I had the occasion to meet two groups of senior citizens in Edmonton, all of whose members were pioneers, totalling some 600. Not a single one of these hardy pioneers complained that 6 per cent and 5 per cent increases in the next two years was too little. In fact, they were more concerned about the young men and women who are unemployed and they wished they could somehow help.
There are many other aspects of this budget that one could debate positively or negatively, but allow me to look backward a little bit. During the decade of the sixties, I worked mostly out of New York and also Arizona in the United States. What a decade the sixties was for North America! The sixties was an era of magic, when we of the technologically trained society held the world in our hands, when technology and the world economy exploded in a decade of development and growth, and human interaction and peace. There seemed to be no limits to our imagination or to our dreams as scientists, engineers and politicians. We were certain that we could change the world in but a few decades and build a paradise on earth.
Then we left the sixties behind and cautiously entered the seventies. I remember writing the following for a speech that I gave to the Man and Resources Conference in Toronto in 1974. In that speech I said:
This century has fostered revolution in science and technology, in the generation and use of energy, in industrial productivity, in population growth, in urbanization and in destructive potential which have buffeted humanity at a rate too quick for the human mind to adequately comprehend and absorb.
The Budget-Mr. Yurko
The spiritual, social and intellectual consequences of these revolutions are profound and not entirely determinable. Our present day cultures are increasingly beset by an oppressive sense of fragmentation and instability. We are beginning to question and even doubt our own continuity as a progressing civilization. We derive from our awesome technological complexity both a confidence of power and a sharp premonition of vulnerability.
Yes, the seventies became a decade of doubt and readjustment both worldwide and in Canada. The western world built a mobile society based on cheap oil. The oil then became expensive, and this triggered a world economic whirlwind which brought inflation, a halt to world economic growth, protectionism and pessimism. In retrospect, Canada would perhaps have been far better off today if we had gone quickly to world energy prices, as the United States did. However, that is wishful thinking.
This pessimism and inwardness catapulted into the eighties with disruptive force and affected Canada so much that today one must ask what has happened to us as Canadians. What has happened to our dreams? What has happened to our ideals? What has happened to our will to be in the forefront of world nations in productivity, in sharing and in helping each other and all the less endowed people of the earth? The great idealism of the sixties and early seventies has crashed, trampled in the wake of our own riches. We lost our initiative, our drive, our determination and even our will to excel both nationally and internationally. We have exchanged political co-operation for political intransigence. Federal-provincial cooperation has given way to upmanship and gamesmanship, although I am encouraged by the posture and attitude of the ten Premiers since the recent first ministers' conference. In particular, I am encouraged by the actions of the Progressive Conservative Premier of Nova Scotia who accepted the federal restraint guidelines.
We have traded productivity and pride of accomplishment for slothfulness and laziness, and now I see labour leaders publicly advocating more of the same as a strategy for fighting restraint. The figures on lost time in the Canadian work force released today are alarming. At times we seem to have become a people without purpose, without compassion and with dubious honesty, and this House is a representative microcosm of the Canadian fabric today. Here we bicker like children and throw verbal frisbees back and forth. We distort, we delay and we belittle each other. The intent is to be destructive and disruptive rather than constructive and efficient. This House has become a place of negativism and pessimism. Through television we provide a daily diet of our characteristics in this House to the nation, and people often ask me when I go back to my constituency if we will ever agree on anything again, as we agreed when we debated the Quebec referendum in this House. "Can you people down there not agree on some direction or on some few things which should be done in this nation?" That is what I am asked.
We must agree, and we must develop a new optimism and a new perspective with regard to the magnificent country we have. So few of us enjoy this wealth like no other peoples of the world. I know every Member of Parliament deals with immigration problems in his constituency because there is not a soul

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Cyr
anywhere in the world who does not want to emigrate to this country which has such vast potential. We must find the enthusiasm, the desire and the optimism necessary to build this nation again. We must agree to work together to solve the economic malaise facing and punishing all Canadians, and I know we can do better from here on than we have done in the past.
