subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may say it is a pleasure and a privilege to be taking part in this budget debate. I would like to take a few minutes to talk about those of us who were expecting miracles and those Canadians who are convinced that all the problems our country is facing today are the result of errors, past and present, of the Government of Canada. I also have some comments on the state of the economy in the riding of Gaspe and I shall explain how weak international markets are responsible for the shutdown of several factories, and that the world economic situation must improve if we are to revive our copper, paper and seafood industries.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an editorial by Claude LeVergne, published on July 4 under the heading: "The budget as a reminder of reality". It says, and I quote:
In fact, the Finance Minister, who, it is generally conceded, had very little room to manoeuvre, opted for an economic sermon rather than radical corrective measures. To that extent, his speech may prove to have been worth while provided it was understood. Without wishing to overestimate this last budget, the fact is that opposing factions both inside and outside Parliament have been extrapolating the proposed measures in a very negative manner, without actually suggesting any real alternative solutions. It is always easy to say too little too late, but it would seem to be incumbent on the critics to come up with real guidelines for corrective action, which they have failed to do. If Mr. MacEachen succeeds in making Canadians aware of the present crisis situation, his speech will not have been in vain.
Mr. Speaker, all around us today, we see signs of great upheaval which have been characteristic of the North American scene during the last twenty years. We have seen the spectacular growth of an economy with an almost limitless capacity for expanding production suddenly turn into an inflationary monster gone completely out of control. The goal of the June budget is to restore public confidence in a future when inflation will subside and new investment will create the jobs we so urgently need. Mr. Speaker, the appeal for national solidarity made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) must be heard by all Canadians. Many, far too many people, including politicians, businessmen, labour leaders and educators, are claiming that any system of government that has failed to get rid of unemployment, exploitation and inflation is a failure and should be eliminated.
According to this kind of reasoning, we should destroy all our hospitals and shoot all the doctors because they have failed to wipe out disease. Mr. Speaker, before destroying one system, I think they should suggest another that will be able to resolve the problems of unemployment, exploitation, undue profits and inflation. As Leo Rosten said: "Anyone can
promise Utopia if he does not specify a program." Our system of government is ideal, and the objective of the Minister of Finance will be achieved and our way of life preserved, provided enough Canadians show sufficient concern for the national interest in their daily decisions. In the years to come, Canadians will have to spend more time and energy on resolving the nation's problems. Excessive wage demands and unreasonable profits increase the cost of goods, and consumers will have to pay the bill. Canadians must condemn every purely egotistical decision. Indifference to poverty is inexcusable in a society that is dedicated to the dignity of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to discuss the economic situation in the riding of Gaspe and the distributive justice we are asking for, which is the philosophy of the Liberal Party but is too often ignored by certain departments. The needs of each community and its individual members are multiple and complex. They include basic requirements such as survival, as well as more complex psychological aspirations such as personal development. These needs truly represent the basic goals of individual Canadians. Socially, they correspond to two essential goals, namely well-being and equity. All the intermediate goals help toward meeting these basic aspirations. Well-being is measured by the extent to which material, sociocultural and other needs are met. On the other hand, equity consists in the fair redistribution of the assets of society. It is probably the idea of equal opportunities which best illustrates the most significant and universally accepted concept of equity at the present time. Its aim is to provide everyone with the same opportunities to achieve well-being. Another aspect of equity is the equality of results.
In the Gaspe area, and especially in my constituency of Gaspe, we have neither equal opportunities nor equal results. The standard of living in a country or a region depends on the income of the population, the cost of living and the economic benefits. We are well aware that we have many non-economic benefits in the Gaspe area. However, the average salary is 40 per cent lower in that area than in Quebec as a whole. In the Gaspe region, the majority of the experienced labour force works at unskilled jobs in the resource sector, for instance, in the mining and forest industries. In fact, the Gaspe region has proportionately twice as many workers in these industries as the Quebec average.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the present world recession is felt more badly in economically weak and disadvantaged regions where the economy is supported by the resource industries. In my constituency of Gaspe, the regional unemployment rate is 40 per cent, among the highest in Canada. To make the situation even more confused, many industries are now experiencing financial problems. On June 30, Mines Madeleine Ltee closed down their mining operations in Sainte-Anne-des-Monts. This is a permanent closure which has thrown 110 people out of work. The Marsoui sawmill has been
July 8, 1982

closed for 18 months. Over 100 workers are now unemployed, in addition to 125 forest workers. Gaspesia Ltee of Chandler and Mines Gaspe Ltee of Murdochville are closing down temporarily because of newspaper and copper stock surpluses. A total of over 4,000 workers are directly affected by these temporary shutdowns.
In view of the economic situation, manpower centres do not find it advisable to set up relocation committees for workers who have lost their jobs since mines and plants are closing down everywhere. The tourist industry is also very important in the Gaspe region. I am told that there were 25 per cent fewer tourists in June 1982 than in June 1981. Mr. Speaker, I urge all Canadians to visit the Gaspe area this summer because prices are very reasonable there and, as you know, the people are very hospitable. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, even though the Gaspe constituency is economically depressed, the people there still enjoy life and are eager to work. The job creation and economic development initiatives announced by the Minister of Finance will certainly improve the situation for the Gaspe people, but more than stopgap measures are needed. The Industry Development and Industry and Labour Adjustment Programs are two initiatives which could help our regional economy to recover if the required infrastructures were in place. The people of the Gaspe area agree that they have to share the burden and the responsibility of getting Canada out of the recession, slowing down inflation and increasing productivity. Many economists have explained that the lack of social capital, that is the infrastructures, is the main reason behind the lagging economic development in Gaspe and other similar regions. Here is how I would sum up my proposal: there can never be equity among individuals and a truly just society unless the Government of Canada implements measures which are better tailored to meet regional needs and peculiarities.
It is of the utmost importance that governments set up mechanisms and infrastructures in regions such as the riding of Gaspe so that Canadians not be exclusively consumers, but producers as well. The people of Gaspe want a place under the sun in our beautiful and great country and they urge the governments to subsidize employment rather than unemployment.
The budget refers to a program aimed at boosting the building industry. I dare hope that it is only the first of many more stages. We in the riding of Gaspe have to cope with inflation like everybody else and, as I said at the outset, we have to think in terms of adequate infrastructures to spur the economic recovery of our region and encourage investors to set up shop there.
We have nothing against massive investments in such designated centres as Montreal and Quebec City. Still, the products of Gaspe must find their way to those centres and that is why we urgently need adequate infrastructures. Right now, I have in mind the improvements that will have to be made to the airports of Sainte-Anne-des-Monts, Pabos and Gaspe so as to promote the industrial expansion of those regions and centres. I also have in mind the construction of a
The Budget-Mr. Cyr
multiple purpose harbour in the Sainte-Anne-des-Monts and Cap-Chat region, as well as the improvement and upgrading of harbour facilities in Gaspe. Finally, what can I say about the small marinas along the coast of the Gaspe Peninsula? A cursory examination of existing facilities and the lack of infrastructures throughout the region vividly reflect the fact that fishermen are so hard pressed to earn a living at their trade.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to ask the government for more money than we can rightfully expect. However, within the scope of the programs mentioned in the June 28 budget and others already implemented, I would like that very careful consideration be given to the reallocation of available funds while keeping in mind the particular needs of the people of Gaspe and especially the needs of the whole electoral riding of Gaspe which I represent. That is what is called distributive justice. A good many citizens of the Gaspe area look favourably upon the budget proposals aimed at appreciably lowering the interest rates. Whether buying a new house or beginning construction before next December 31, the first-time home buyer will be eligible for a $3,000 grant. Small businesses as well will be able to get working capital for development and construction at 4 percentage points under the prevailing rate, and fishermen will also qualify for the reduced rate to finance new capital equipment. All those people greatly appreciate the effort of the government and will certainly benefit from those budget measures. As far as 1 know, two businesses in the riding of Gaspe have already applied to avail themselves of the rates at 4 percentage points lower than prevailing rates. Those measures will certainly give a boost to businessmen, fishermen and farmers anxious to run a sound operation, and they will dispel their fears about risks and overly high investment costs.
Mr. Speaker, we all know the major cause of unemployment-the idling construction industry.
The construction industry's multiplier is 3.5. This means that for each dollar invested in the building industry, we are expending $3.50 in other industries such as logging, mining, furniture, textiles, appliances, etc. I am therefore happy that the budget includes various types of proposals to help to stimulate housing. The five-point package may not have in the Gaspe Peninsula the social and economic impact they will have in other areas. However, it will help the lumber industry to recover and provide jobs in sawmills and logging operations.
There is also a $30 million funding increase for the Canada Home Renovation Plan (CHRP), a program that certainly will have a very significant impact in the Gaspe Peninsula as soon as people in that area are aware of the terms.
And of course, Mr. Speaker, the needs are great. People are willing, but there must also be a political will for the whole of Gaspe rather than just one or two cities east of Quebec to experience harmonious development. This is the distributive justice of the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker.
Recently, I was reminded of Hamlet's monologue that goes like this:
To be, or not to be: that is the question:
19140

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Ellis
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune.
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them?
People in Gaspe have always had to fight to earn their living. I feel 1 am speaking on their behalf when I say that once more they would be ready to go all out to get the most from the prevailing situation to ensure the welfare of their community. However, they want to make sure that government authorities, under the budget tabled June 28, will ensure that the maximum available funds are used for a consistent economic recovery and reallocation of funds, based on the particular conditions that make Gaspe an area where resource development is slow because of a blatant lack of infrastrutures in various fields. Mr. Speaker, once more we are faced with a challenge. It is the duty of every Canadian to do his part to obtain the security we all are looking for. This budget is a call to reality that every Canadian should answer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not taken part in some of the major debates in this House recently, for a number of reasons. The debate on the National Energy Program was skilfully handled by some of my colleagues who have a particular expertise in that area. In addition, I found it necessary to spend a great deal of my time working with individuals and companies in my constituency in an attempt to shield them from the vagaries of this government. Even then I was unsuccessful in my attempt to commit the government to buying better quality, Canadian-built and lower-priced equipment, rather than Japanese.
As for the debate now taking place on this excuse for a budget presented to us on June 28, there have been a number of speakers from my party who have very capably covered the major points and it would be quite easy for me to sit back and allow them to speak on this occasion. Indeed, I would be quite comfortable with most of what has been said to date by my colleagues. There is, however, a facet of this budget which has not, to my knowledge, been dealt with.
My colleagues, by and large, have dealt with the over-all impact of the budget on Canadians. Let me deal for a few moments with its impact on individuals and attempt to add a human scale to this latest travesty by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Let me attempt to break it down and point out what it means to individuals in the riding of Prince Edward-Hastings, a small but I expect typical riding in eastern Ontario.
We have been told that the budget deficit for 1982-83 is a figure of $19.6 billion. That is just a number, Mr. Speaker, one which is very hard for the majority of my constituents to reconcile. I know that I cannot think of it in terms of real dollars. However, when you break it down to an amount of $840 for every man, woman and child, newborn or centenarian, it is a number I can relate to.
Prior to this budget the national debt incurred by the Liberal government was $135 billion, another figure which is just as difficult to understand. It is more manageable when broken down to $5,700 for each person. For people living in the city of Belleville, where I live, this means that the deficit the federal government will incur this year in their name alone amounts to $29.5 million. It is interesting to note that that is exactly the same amount that the entire city administration will spend this year.
Let us look at that figure again, Mr. Speaker. All of the money collected by the city of Belleville this year to pay for the entire administration-the city council, staff, police and firemen, snowplowing, garbage collection, road repairs, street cleaning and maintenance, and the myriad of services provided by the city-will be equalled by that part of the federal deficit owed by the citizens of Belleville. Does anyone really believe there is any comparison between the services received by the people from the municipalities and those from the federal government? I am confident that most would agree they get a far better deal from their city.
Over the years the city of Belleville, like most municipalities, has spent money on capital projects on which in their wisdom they have deferred payment. These include major roads, bridges and other large capital expenditures. This means the city has a debt, and it is roughly $13 million. The federal government has also not paid its way over the past few years and the consequences are, as I said a few moments ago, a debt of $135 billion. In terms of the people in the city of Belleville, that works out to $200 million, or 15 times the debt Belleville has incurred for its own capital works budget. Once again, does anyone really think that there is any benefit to the people of Belleville from that particular debt?
Let me take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to relate the figures to those rural parts of the Quinte district which I represent. If you apply this year's federal deficit to the residents of Prince Edward County, they owe $19 million on top of the $131 million already incurred by the federal government. Compare that to the total Prince Edward County budget for this year of less than $4 million. For Hastings County, if the current deficit were going to be paid this year, it would amount to $88 million. The debt incurred by the Liberal government on their behalf before this budget was some $600 million, and that is still unpaid. These are astronomical figures, very difficult to understand, and even more difficult when you consider that the entire Hastings County budget for 1982 is only $14.5 million. In all of these cases that I have outlined, these are just the deficits. These are just the amounts which the federal government has spent but has not collected.
The federal government spends money at the rate of $214 million a day, $9 million an hour or $150,000 a minute. Thus, when the federal government spends, it spends in two hours and eight minutes as much as the whole of the city of Belleville spends in one year. In 17 minutes and 20 seconds the federal government spends all that Picton will spend in one year. In
July 8, 1982

five minutes and 15 seconds the federal government spends the entire budget of Deseronto. The federal government would spend the entire budget of the little village of Tweed, through which many members from Ontario drive on their way to Ottawa, in four minutes. The federal government would gobble up the budget of the pretty village of Wellington located on the south shore overlooking Lake Ontario in Prince Edward County in two minutes and 28 seconds.
How does the federal government spend this money? Some of it goes to items such as Mirabel airport. Mirabel airport has cost the taxpayers of Canada some $700 million to date. That is equivalent to the budget for the whole of the city of Belleville, the whole of Prince Edward County and the whole of Hastings County, not just that portion I represent. It includes the portions represented by my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) as well as by my colleague the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox-Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet). The cost of operating Mirabel airport would be the equivalent of covering all of Hastings County budgets for 15 years.
The federal government has an advertising budget of nearly $235 million. In other words, the federal government spends on advertising alone more than the city of Belleville spends in its whole budget for eight years. Perhaps it is better to leave those figures in the impersonal billions of dollars, because when I get them down to real terms it frightens the hell out of me.
Let me try to relate some of the major items in the budget in more human terms that would apply to the people of a riding such as Prince Edward-Hastings. Many of my colleagues have made the point that senior citizens have been hit hard, in fact hit twice by this budget, once by having their pensions dein-dexed and second by having their income tax deindexed, resulting in their having to pay higher income taxes. I suppose the Minister of Finance knew that those people in their sixties, seventies and eighties were those who came through the dirty thirties; they know what a real depression is like and would probably not complain as much as some younger ones would.
Let me tell the Minister of Finance that these are the same people who have watched this Liberal government over the years, have watched its wasteful spending, have seen the lack of responsibility, have heard the disparaging remarks made about the Parliament of Canada by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and have seen cabinet minister after cabinet minister show favouritism to one part of Canada over another. They know how much a $20 million contract to a Belleville firm would mean, or what $30 million in assistance would mean to a Windsor factory. Those things would provide jobs. Our senior citizens also know there was no chance of those things happening because the businesses are located in Ontario.
Yes, the senior citizens are the ones who know how to tighten their belts better than most Canadians. But also better than most Canadians, they probably appreciate that it would not have been necessary had it not been for the action of this government.
The Budget-Mr. Ellis
When it comes to restraint, this government has long since forgotten what the word means. I want to go on record as being quite prepared to see cuts made in the salaries of Members of Parliament and senior civil servants. As far as Members of Parliament are concerned, since there are so few it is a token gesture in any event. Senior civil servants, many of whom make twice as much as Members of Parliament and who are fully protected against inflation, could stand a cut both in salary and in real numbers.
How can there be any credibility left for a government whose projections could be so wrong? We have all heard that projections made in the November 12 budget are now admitted by the Minister of Finance to be in error. The authors of those projections should have been fired. Instead, they received major raises.
Why would any businessman want to invest in Canada? Whether it is a Canadian businessman or one from offshore- who would first of all have to fight all of the FIRA regulations-these businessmen have no idea what the tax climate is going to be from day to day. Businessmen who were operating under one set of rules prior to November 12 had those rules changed, even though the legislation was never brought in. In June of this year another change came about. It is doubtful whether that legislation will be passed before another budget is brought in later this year in the fall.
Let me return again to the city of Belleville. When I was mayor of that city I had to prepare a five-year budget for its citizens. I know that my successors continue to do the same thing. Thus it is that if someone wished to know what the city of Belleville is going to spend over the next few years, he or she need only go to the city hall and ask a competent civil servant or a dedicated member of council to get an answer. With over 500,000 civil servants, should the Government of Canada be allowed to do less?
The federal government spends a lot of time advertising what it is going to do and spends a lot of money on programs to provide jobs. What the federal government should do is emulate one young farmer in Prince Edward County who last week alone had nearly 400 students on his payroll on a parttime basis. He had no help from the federal government. He and his wife had to stay up nearly all of Thursday night to make out the pay cheques for his employees. These cheques were in payment for work ranging from a few hours to a full week. The total payroll was over $10,000. If the federal government would spend only a portion of the money it wastes in helping farmers and small-business men do their jobs, there would be far less unemployment.
And how about a small successful businessman in Belleville, who by supplying merchandise at fair prices and excellent service has built a good business over the past 25 years? Even now with a much weakened economy his sales this year will probably equal those of last year. The problem is that with the extra costs imposed on him by all levels of government he will show a loss in his operations this year. He must cut back his staff. He must take advantage of work-sharing programs in order to stay alive, and he will stay alive only with no profit

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Gray
and little incentive to continue. Is this any way to treat a businessman who has dedicated his entire life to building his business, to hiring and training people and to providing benefits for a number of employees? Is this how to provide incentives for prospective businessmen?
This government has lied to the people of Canada in so many different ways that it is difficult to enumerate them all. Can one really believe that the budget deficit will be only $19.6 billion, given the track record of ministers of finance to date? Would a person really start a new business knowing that he has to compete with the federal government for available dollars in order to run that business? Could one plan one's retirement knowing that one's pension is at the whim of this government? Would you even buy a car, Mr. Speaker, knowing that this government two years ago said that an 18-cent increase in the price of gasoline was too high? The answer, of course, to all of those questions is a flat no.
The few stop-gap measures in this budget that are of some value may well be turned around before the end of this year. Nowhere in the budget does it say that the statements in it are the policy of the federal government and will remain so. There is really only one answer that taxpayers can give this government. It is very simple. For the sake of Canada, for the sake of all Canadians, and in the name of God, this government should go. It should get out and let someone else do the job.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that by this time in the budget debate Canadians will be reacting with dismay to the kind of rhetoric which we have been hearing from hon. members opposite. While I realize that we refer to hon. members opposite as the opposition, it seems in this case that "opposition" has meant anything but the constructive alternatives which one expects in our parliamentary system. Instead, members of the opposition are like artists who use only black paint; an unusual concept, perhaps, but difficult even to know when the work is completed, let alone what it is meant to convey.
Certainly Canada, along with the rest of the industrialized world, has serious economic problems. Equally obvious was that for these difficulties to be overcome, a course for Canadians to follow had to be charted. An example of leadership had to be given, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) certainly described that course and set out that example of leadership in his budget.
Now, we do not claim that pointing the way to the solution of our country's problems in the budget presented last week immediately solves those problems, as some opposition members wish Canadians to believe is possible. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said in his recent interview with La Presse of Montreal before the budget, he has no alternatives. In his speech in this debate he certainly proved this to be absolutely true. In reviewing the remarks of opposition members in this debate, there have been the usual kinds of contradictions-at one and the same time calling for increased expenditures and urging a reduction in the deficit.
The budget proposes a balanced route to full recovery, one that calls on Canadians to work together. It calls on those in a better position to do so to aid those most in need, as Canadians have done on so many occasions in our past history. The government in the budget is pointing the way by setting an example for others which I believe must and will be followed. The budget outlined the basic choice-working together for economic recovery or having to continue on a course of high costs, high inflation and lack of international competitiveness, efficiency and productivity.
In a world in which Canada would be isolated from all around us, we might well see our problems dramatically reduced without action by government and the private sector working together; but we do not live in such a world. We are part of the global economy and, as such, we suffer to a substantial degree from the problems of others. Within these kinds of constraints, the government has presented a program in the budget aimed at restoring the Canadian economy while protecting those most in need.
One could say that one of our country's problems is that our successes-and there are many-are obscured by the more strident, the more fearful and the less confident among us, especially those on the other side of the House. Certainly the budget does not ignore the general problems of our economy. The program proposed by the Minister of Finance directs help to those most seriously affected, and it urges everyone to contribute to the solution through government, business and labour working together. The budget could not and did not try to do everything for everyone, but it has asked that everyone do their part. This was in the firm belief that Canada's success is based upon all of us working together in a sense of solidarity and sharing.
I believe that request to be a positive aspect. There are those who speak only of the restraint which is required while ignoring that the reasons the restraint has been requested are to increase assistance and support for those in need, particularly those seeking employment, and to help get the entire economy back on a track of productivity and growth.
Much has been said in this debate about the deficit. We recognize the deficit to be a serious matter. We have not agreed with those who say that the deficit should be increased even further. Also we have not agreed with those who call for steps to lower substantially the deficit at this time, because to do so would only mean pulling substantial purchasing power out of an economy where market demand is already far too weak. It would mean putting even tighter restraint on an economy in which growth of gross national product has already stalled and needs to be encouraged.
Our deficit increase came from the operation of automatic stabilizers in our government expenditure and revenue system. Government tax revenues fell as corporate profits and personal incomes fell. The government spent more but mainly on programs such as unemployment insurance and job creation. Without the operation of automatic stabilizers, the effects of
July 8, 1982

the recession would be worse, the hardship even more severe. The funds provided in the budget will be spent on productive activities to create jobs, to combine with private sector initiatives and investment, and to provide needed assistance to sectors like small businesses, farms and fisheries. As an economic recovery comes about, the basis for correction of our deficit situation will be there as well. As profits and incomes improve, government tax revenues will also improve. As more people get off the unemployment rolls, expenditures on programs like unemployment insurance will decrease.
We have in this budget a number of measures aimed at directly assisting the recovery of the economy. Thus the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) set out measures described generally in the budget aimed at greatly improving the housing sector. These measures will have a tremendous multiplier effect, encouraging not only the construction of houses but also activating sectors such as appliances, furniture, textiles and forest products. These measures will be the source of more than 100,000 jobs. They will also provide additional help to those who could be spending an excessive amount of their income on home renovations or on renewal of their mortgages and the interest costs involved therein.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has given details of the measures generally set out in the budget aimed at direct job creation through government programs which will have the effect of maintaining incomes while the economy recovers and permanent jobs are created through private sector activity.
In addition, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) has provided a more detailed description of the budget measures to provide new assistance to small businessmen, fishermen and farmers through the new program of direct grants aimed at reducing the interest costs of money borrowed for new capital expenditure by up to four percentage points.
The measures to help the housing sector, to help home owners deal with high mortgage costs and to help workers maintain income through participation in government job creation programs are aimed at bridging the gap before implementation can take place of the far-reaching and very innovative proposals for new kinds of measures for all lenders of savings and purchasers of shares in Canadian companies to help them be free of tax on the portion of their interest or their gain represented by inflation. These new measures would make it possible for small business people, farmers and fishermen to obtain funds at interest rates several percentage points lower than prevailing market rates. I am confident the government will want to implement these measures as soon as their feasibility and design are confirmed by the special private sector committee headed by Pierre Lortie, president of the Montreal Stock Exchange.
1 want to ask the House to give special attention to the programs in the budget which add some $300 million to the economic and regional development envelope to assist the
The Budget-Mr. Gray
private sector in the creation of long term, permanent jobs through existing programs like the enterprise development program, the defence industry productivity program, the regional development fund and the program in support of technology-enhanced productivity.
There are a number of good examples that can help to demonstrate why this funding has been added and to illustrate the potential of such funding. Just look back, Mr. Speaker, at some of the announcements I have made over the past five or six weeks. 1 announced that Control Data of Montreal, with the assistance of the enterprise development program, would be developing a new super mini-main frame computer with a world product mandate for its production in Canada, and this is expected to create some 600 jobs.
Then, not long afterward, I announced that again with the support of the enterprise development program of my department Mitel of Ottawa would be developing and marketing a new advanced private automatic branch exchange system, the SX-2000. This could well be providing more than 1,000 jobs both in the Ottawa area and Quebec for people making this new advanced product which would provide the nerve centre for equipment in the new offices of the future.
Not long after that I announced that, again with the support of one of my department's programs, the defence industry productivity program, Litton Industries of Toronto would be manufacturing, once again on a world product mandate basis, a new type of inertial guidance system for commercial aircraft using the new ring laser gyro technology, and this is expected to provide some 1,000 jobs. I was happy to take part in the ceremony marking the delivery of the first such system to Aerospatiale of France. Incidentially, this indicates how we already have the potential for leadership and competitive access to world markets for equipment like those connected with aerospace, electronics and the telecommunications sector.
Just a few days ago I announced that Leigh Instruments of Carleton Place, not far from Ottawa, would be making some very important new components for the new CF-18 fighter plane in association with Lear Siegler of the United States, again with the help of the defence industry productivity program of my department. This is also expected to create a substantial number of new jobs.
What we are talking about here is assistance to lever high-quality additional jobs and advanced technology activity in ways that support new Canadian-controlled advanced technology firms and, yes, foreign-controlled firms operating here on a world product mandate basis which are bringing substantial benefits in terms of jobs, technology and exports to the Canadian economy.
When I refer to developing our own economy I think it important to refer to the role of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. There are those who continuously and perhaps-although I hope not-even deliberately misunderstand or misrepresent the agency and its function. 1 want the House to remember that FIRA has served to ensure that the limited areas of foreign investment it deals with are of significant

The Budget-Mr. Gray
benefit to Canada. That is its basic mandate. 1 would hope that there is no one in the House or in the country who would wish foreign investment to be otherwise for the Canadian economy.
The recent changes announced in the budget, changes of an administrative nature, are based on the work of an interdepartmental committee under my direction, in a process of administrative review that was announced in the economic development document tabled with the last budget. I have long believed that administrative improvement in FIRA was essential to the efficient and effective functioning of the FIRA process. My work as minister has certainly strengthened this belief I held before I assumed this present responsibility.
As the Minister of Finance said in his budget:
The Foreign Investment Review Act must be administered to adhere to the objectives established by Parliament. Its procedures must be timely and efficient. In particular, efforts must be made to avoid red tape and extended delays.
The measures announced have been developed to deal with these issues. We do not want to have administrative impediments making it difficult for FIRA promptly and efficiently to help the government on behalf of the Canadian people to ensure that, to the extent it is needed, investment from abroad is in fact of significant benefit to Canada. We certainly welcome such investment, but we want to encourage and ensure that it is of significant benefit for Canadians. I suggest that the rhetoric about FIRA somehow frightening off that investment is simply that, just empty rhetoric not based on fact because the number of applications to FIRA has been steadily rising. The United States department of commerce said in a recent survey that affiliates of U.S. parent firms in Canada intend to invest more in this country than in any other country in which subsidiaries of U.S. parent companies operate.
As many have said, businesses operate best when they have confidence. However, I believe the essential element to business confidence is confidence that they will be able to make a profit. The Foreign Investment Review Act is certainly not intended to be a roadblock to investment aimed at creating employment which does not simply operate to perpetuate the branch plant environment that has been of so much concern to so many people.
We have a responsibility to Canadians to ensure that the Canadian economy is vibrant and growing and certainly, as in the past, the Foreign Investment Review Act which was a mandate created by Parliament will play a very important and positive role in that regard in the future.
I want to conclude by reminding the House of the basic concepts of the very important budget presented by the Minister of Finance a few days ago. First, the minister pointed out that we must work together in order to enter an era of growth based upon 6 per cent increases in costs in Canada. We must move away from the present 12 per cent world of inflation and into a 6 per cent world of growth. We must operate on a basis of government leadership and example. We are certainly doing this. We must operate on the basis of government, labour and business working together in a co-operative and consultative way. As well, we are certainly doing this. We
July 8, 1982
must make major efforts not only in support simply of direct job creation, important as that is, but in support of efforts by the private sector to create permanent, long-term jobs. We are making a major commitment of government funds toward this purpose.
I think it has been clearly demonstrated during this debate that the budget presented by the Minister of Finance a few days ago is a courageous and much needed effort to chart a course of leadership to bring the Canadian economy back on a path of full growth and development and all that this means for Canadians and their families. Therefore, in order to help Canadians achieve this goal, I ask the House to vote conclusively and overwhelmingly in support of this budget in the interests of all Canadians and future generations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the June budget. It never ceases to amaze me how the Liberal cabinet would put the entire blame for the
July 8, 1982

nation's problems today on the nine months that the Progressive Conservative Party was in power. One would think that the whole nation collapsed during that nine-month period whereas in actual fact it took nine months to find out all of the graft, corruption and evil that they had hidden away in the closets. They were so numerous it took nine months to count the skeletons in the closet before we could even start to address the problem. Fortunately for them they were able, in coalition with the New Democratic Party, to bring down the Clark government, and once again the cloak of secrecy has fallen over the affairs of the nation. They can continue to add skeletons where the others lie.
I want to speak to the Canadian people and other members of this House about the underlying philosophy of this budget. Canadians have now come to realize that there is an economic philosophy in this country. The great Liberal Party of years past has now become really a party like the NDP. It is really a philosophy of socialization.
There is a difference between the parties, and I want to discuss that. Regretfully, Canadians now have to pay the price for having elected successive Liberal-NDP coalition governments. It is a truism that the sins of the fathers are visited upon their children. That is what the Canadian people are suffering today.
It is my thesis that the Liberal Party has changed fundamentally from that party of reform of the early forties and fifties, a party that many people fell in love with because it was going to redistribute and create genuine justice and equity. It no longer is that. It is merely a centralist, socialist and nationalist party. I will show how that has not worked to the benefit of individual working Canadians.
Ordinary working Canadians are now injured and in a position where they are worse off then they were in 1968. That should always be where we start because the true test of any government should be the condition of ordinary Canadians.
I challenge any member of the Liberal Party or the NDP to name even one socialist state where the ordinary people are better off than the Canadian people were in 1968 but not today. In 1968 we had a very low unemployment rate. There was basically full employment. The unemployment at that time of 3 per cent to 4 per cent was the ordinary case of people moving to new jobs. Youth unemployment was low. Inflation was 4.2 per cent. The bank rate was 7.5 per cent. Government spending totalled about $12 billion compared to financial requirements today of over $17 billion. The government deficit was small.
However, at that time we had a solid country. This was an exciting nation. 1 graduated in 1968. All the young people had jobs to go to. This was truly a dynamic nation. There was the unity of Expo '67. We had a health insurance program and a medicare program that was sound. We had post-secondary education that was expanding. It was really a treat to be part of it. We had old age security, the Canada Pension Plan and a solid private entrepreneurship base that was creating wealth, bringing in technology and developing modern ways to search for oil in the west.
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
We had a research and development component that was adding new cereals, grains and alfalfas. For example, canola has returned billions of dollars to this country. We had all of that in 1968. We were respected internationally and we were clearly charging ahead.
Then this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected who, by his own admission, is a socialist. The Prime Minister has never denied that. Members on the government side try to deny that, but not once has the Prime Minister. He has always been straight up and honest with Canadians. He honestly believes that a small cabinet and a bureaucracy around it can make decisions that are far wiser than having millions of individual entrepreneurs make those decisions. One need only review his writings at university to find that. He has never denied it. Not once has the Prime Minister denied any of his writings, and nor should he because he has never tried to deceive the Canadian people. He has always told them the situation exactly.
Since that date we have a steady march toward government involvement. That is what socialism is. It is the taking over of the marketplace where millions and millions of decisions are made and reducing it so that the decisions are made by one group. That is a government in power. They have done that by way of Crown corporations. Over the last 14 years the number of Crown corporations has increased by well over 200 so that the total now is over 400 Crown corporations in the country.
One need only look at Bill C-124, the government restraint bill, which lists all of the Crown corporations, all of the regulatory agencies and other agencies that respond to government, to find that the bulk of them came in during the last ten to 14 years. During that period the nation has seen a steady decline in vitality. I do not believe it is an accident that Canada faces the problems it does today. It is the direct result of the centralization of power and the nationalization of decision making in this nation.
At the same time, the tax system has changed dramatically. Under the old system, if a person started a business and incurred an expense in the process, it was automatically deductible against whatever income the business earned. That is not the case today. Today all of the money goes into the centre. We must come to Ottawa with hat in hand and on one knee. The government will decide whether you get a grant. That is a different system from what we had before.
Previously in the oil industry you would bring together a skilled group of engineers and scientists that would do the seismic work. They decided where to drill based on the scientific data. When they drilled they would deduct the cost from the revenue if they found oil. Now they first have to come to Ottawa. Depending on where they are going to drill and depending on their rate of Canadian ownership, they might get a grant that goes from 90 per cent if they drill where the governments wants them to, down to less than 50 per cent if they drill where they decide. We are going to have wells being drilled in areas where the government wants them drilled, not necessarily where the oil is. When you drill a dry hole, which averages about $5 million, that money is gone. There is no

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
recovery from a dry well. The billions of dollars that will be lost to this nation as a result of that process is a tragedy. It makes anyone who knows the oil industry weep.
The ordinary Canadian citizen is always at the end of the whip. No matter how the government tries to say they can pull money out of the air, that money basically comes from Canadian citizens. If you look at the statistics on the amount of money that is put up by citizens, Mr. Speaker, you realize that we truly are back to the days of feudalism and that we are all serfs. A slave is really just someone who is taxed 100 per cent. Therefore, as an economic creature, all of his economic rent goes into the hands of another person who decides how to spend it. The slave has no decision-making powers.
That is what is happening today. If one adds up municipal, provincial and federal taxes, one will find that well over 50 per cent of one's economic rent goes into the hands of other people who decide how it should be spent rather than you. That is the difference between the parties. The Liberal Party, which is clearly with the NDP, very much wants that economic power to come into the centre and then the cabinet will decide how it will be distributed, as compared to our party which would leave it with millions and millions of individual people. We believe that the collective result of millions and millions of decisions is far wiser than one made in the middle.
Then there is the deficit. Clearly, $20 billion is almost intolerable. We then find Bill C-125, which the government wants us to approve, a bill which would let it borrow $11 billion. Just a few days ago I stood up to oppose a previous bill which would have allowed the government to borrow $6 billion. I suppose that in another three months it will be up to another $15 billion, because the government now must go out into the marketplace. Over and above all the billions of dollars it collects from people through income tax and other direct taxes, whether sales taxes or corporate taxes, the government must go out and raise an additional $17 billion. It is no wonder that interest rates are high, because the government needs the money. Therefore it jacks up interest rates. If we did not have the deficit we would not be paying the interest. That is the lesson that people have to learn in their own lives. If one does not get into debt, one does not have to pay the interest.
Where are we? As a result of this administration, we now find, in 1982, that health insurance is in real trouble. We find that the medicare system is failing. We find that post-secondary education is weak and getting weaker when at this time it should be stronger. In terms of the international sphere, never have we more needed trained, high technology people, yet in the last fiscal agreement the federal government cut its contributions.
We are losing indexing of old age security payments. People receiving benefits under the Canada Pension Plan are in real jeopardy because their premiums came into Ottawa, but did Ottawa put that money into a fund which would generate wealth for them? No. It lent the money out to the provinces and at a very low rate of interest, the theory being that when more people were taking out than putting in, the provinces
would pay back the loans to the federal government which would then distribute it under the Canada Pension Plan. But seven provinces east of Saskatchewan all have enormous deficits. They took the money, spent it on programs and do not have it now. They are in a deficit position. Therefore, we are in the absurd position that when the pay-out from the Canada Pension Plan is greater than the premium income, the provinces will be called to pay the debt back. Where will they get the money? They will have to increase taxes on the very same people who in earlier years paid their premiums. So they will be doubly taxed. It is incredible but that is the burden the Liberal administration has put on this nation.
Again, in 1982 unemployment affects 1.3 million people. Canada is no longer an exciting, dynamic place for young people to come out to as it was in 1968 when I was graduating along with many other members. There is a real uncertainty among our youth because their unemployment rate is 17.5 per cent nationally. It is over 40 per cent in some specific provinces.
We then get back to the National Energy Program which single-handedly destroyed the most exciting and dynamic industry in the west, one which would have carried this whole nation through these tough times because thousands and thousands of young people were coming from across the country to take jobs in Alberta. Had that Alsands plant gone ahead and had the Cold Lake plant gone ahead, with the petro-chemical upgrading plants they could all have had jobs. Now there are no jobs. Interestingly enough, it is the young people from Ontario and Quebec who are having to go back to their homes and say that they do not have jobs, although there is still enough economic development in Alberta to absorb the Alberta graduates. So ironically it is not hurting the very people whose province the energy program has hurt.
Of course, from a narrow, selfish point of view, Albertans would be entitled to say: "The longer the oil stays in the ground, the better it will be for our children and for our grandchildren". The only reason they were producing that oil in the first place was for the good of the nation, not for any selfish need on their part. Inflation is now at 11.8 per cent. The deficit is at $20 billion. What does that do? Governments operate around balanced budgets. Therefore, in bad times they would go into debt in order to make the capital investments that would make capital available for industry to create jobs and then, in the good times, the tax revenue would flow and they would pay back the debt so that they could go around that zero line. Sometimes there is a deficit in good years; it is paid back and a surplus may even be built up. Then in bad years it goes down. What happens when one gets into a deficit position is that one will always go around the line.
Now the Liberals are going around the line of annual deficits of about $20 billion and a net deficit of about $20 billion and a net deficit of something over $100 billion. The problem is that one is still going around that line, but out of the revenue one must pay interest on that deficit. Therefore, something like 25 per cent or 26 per cent of every revenue
July 8, 1982

dollar is simply servicing the debt. What that does is to concentrate wealth. People who have money in the bank were doing just fine. I have invested my cash. Some people have even sold assets and put the money in the bank because that wealth is concentrating the interest on $100 billion. What that does is create a class society. It simply means that the rich become incredibly rich, the poor have no chance of getting out and the middle class is being eroded from the bottom. It is becoming smaller and smaller. Pretty soon we will be in a situation similar to that found in India and all the other Third World countries where there is either a fascist dictatorship on the top or a socialist-communist dictatorship. There will be incredibly rich people and incredibly poor people. Well, that is not what Canada is all about. If one speaks to ordinary citizens, one finds that that is not what they want; but that is exactly what is happening to this nation and it is happening because of deficits.
I can say to hon. members opposite that the parents of those of us from the west learned that lesson, because during the thirties the province of Alberta had to default on provincial bonds and that was such a humiliation to the people of Alberta at that time that they put in a Social Credit government, and British Columbia very quickly followed. There is a public populist feeling that they will not tolerate government deficits.
I come from that milieu, I can see the history of it and I believe that to be correct.
I will be presenting a private member's bill to change the Constitution so that governments cannot take us into deficit positions. For years, the Liberal government has been able to offer programs like this, good programs, but with a low capitalist tax. It says, for example: "Relax; here is the program and your taxes will not change. We will then borrow it all at the same time." First at 10 per cent, then at 15 per cent and then at 20 per cent. Now, over 25 per cent of our revenue services that debt, so we are now getting socialist taxes to meet the socialist programs. But in the meantime people have gone out and bought houses that are too big, they have huge mortgages, they have paid too much for land and they have paid too much for businesses. With the combination of high taxes to meet these programs, they are just falling like flies. There are tens of thousands of bankruptcies in this nation, and that is unnecessary. When a government offers a program, it should be forced to say to the people: "Flere is the program, here is the tax. What do you think? Do you want it?" If that were done, people would give their views and governments would not get themselves into such trouble.
It is no accident that we are where we are. It is not the fault of the United States of America; it is not the fault of the European Economic Community; it is not the fault of the Premiers. We are in trouble because the Canadian people elected a Liberal-NDP coalition. They had the right to do that and that is what they did. That coalition is governing with its majority. I am naturally hopeful that in the next election the people will realize that in the long term the nation should not
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
permit a concentration of power. It does not matter to me whether it is a Liberal government, a Conservative government or an NDP government; any time a nation permits the concentration of power into too few hands, there will be trouble. That is exactly what the battle for Parliament was about. Kings had absolute power. The power of those kings is now exercised by the executive-the cabinet-and the cabinet is supposed to be responsible to all of us. That is the part of our form of government which has failed. Because of party discipline, individual government backbenchers have not stood with sufficient vigour against the tendency of the cabinet to concentrate power.
The alternative thesis is that they agree. Perhaps Liberal backbenchers agree with everything the Cabinet has done. Perhaps they agree with the National Energy Program in total. Perhaps they agree with the budget and its deficit. If that is so, the only solution for the Canadian people is to turf them out on an individual basis. I suppose that is exactly the solution.
What is this socialism about which we talk? Some people laugh and hoot, as if socialists were communist in the sense of Brezhnev and his crew. That is not the model of socialism about which I speak. I speak about socialism as the economic system whereby there is public ownership and control of the means of production. That is exactly what has been happening in this country.
1 explained earlier the operation of the oil industry and that prior to the National Energy Program entrepreneurs made decisions about where they would drill. Now it is government which decides. It is government and bureaucracy which decide where driling will take place. Bill C-85 is legislation to establish a corporation called Canagrex to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agriculture and agricultural food products. This legislation is in exactly the same position as the Petroleum Administration Act some years ago when the government decided it wanted to move into the oil industry. This Canagrex legislation will mean the ultimate takeover of food production in this country. When we have powerful government, what happens is that it causes problems, and the solution is not to have less government but more. As we get more problems, we get more government.
It becomes a circle, and ultimately we end up with a country like Russia. The classic example is eastern Europe, where they used to export food but people now stand in food lines. Bureaucrats and politicians in Russia decide that there will be so many million hectares of wheat, so many million hectares of barley, oats and so on. A mechanism has been put into place whereby seed is distributed to farms at the "right time". But they always forget that mother nature plays a hand. Sometimes there are late rains. On July 15 when farmers should be sowing barley, because some bureaucrat has said they should sow wheat, in goes wheat. Farmers at the state farm level know it will freeze off, and it does. Under our system, if it rains here or hails there, the individual farmer can make the instantaneous decision to change his crop. Therefore, we invariably have a huge surplus, which contributes some $6 billion to our trade balance.

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Thacker
To the extent that Canagrex takes decision-making away from individual farmers we will be in trouble, and 1 have no doubt at all but that Canadians could be standing in food lines too, because when we get beyond the export of cereal grains, Canada is a massive importer of food. It is not at all beyond the realm of possibility that Canadians could be standing in food lines. If there ever is a blockage of that line of trucks coming in from the United States of America, Canadians could be standing in food lines within three days.
Somehow we think we can kick the United States around all the time. We live under its nuclear umbrella, yet we stand up and say we are nuclear free. We forget that we are involved in guidance systems and testing of Cruise missiles. We seem to think we can kick the Americans and still live under their protection. We are going to learn a hard lesson.
The prime vehicle on the road to socialism has been Crown corporations, of which I said there are over 400. In Bill C-124 we can see the details. I explained how we are using the tax system to make us more socialist. Unfortunately, the defect is that socialism simply does not work because the government causes problems and then creates more government to solve them. The classic example I mentioned on an earlier occasion is Petro-Canada. Some years ago it started with $300 million or $400 million. Every year since then it has come back, and the Liberal government has procured hundreds of millions more into it. Direct total investment was some $2 billion cash, but Petro-Canada still was not working so we gave it a 25 per cent back-in provision respecting oil lands in the north. That was not working, so we just outright confiscated 25 per cent of the oil lands from other companies and gave them to Petro-Canada. It is still not working, so now we have the ultimate provision. Every time any citizen drives up to the gas pump, he pays approximately four cents per gallon off the top, which goes to Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada will succeed if it takes every penny out of every Canadian's pocket. It cannot fail because it was created by a political cabinet; it has to succeed. It does not matter whether the cabinet is Liberal, Conservative or NDP; their reputation is at stake, so Petro-Canada will succeed no matter what. As the years go by, we will see more and more money being poured into Petro-Canada, and it simply will not work.
Another way governments hurt people is by reneging on agreements. The classic example is the treatment of federal superannuates by this budget. There are approximately 120,000 retired federal public servants who have average incomes of just over $7,000. The surviving spouses of retired civil servants have average incomes of about $2,100. Those men and women worked 20 or 30 years and paid premiums in order to be entitled to their pensions. That is fair enough; private industry does the same thing. However, federal public servants paid an extra 1 per cent in order to have their pensions indexed. Throughout the course of their lives they gave up an extra 1 per cent of their incomes in order to have protection from inflation in the future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You opposed it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The most recent budget did away with all that. We have confiscated 1 per cent from our retired federal civil servants. It is just gone. There was no point in their having paid it at all. They might as well have paid just the ordinary premium. One might think a government truly committed to equity and fairness would at least say to federal public servants at this time, "We will not collect the 1 per cent from you", but the government will continue to collect the extra 1 per cent during this two-year restraint period. Alternatively, one might think the government would feel some obligation to pay the 1 per cent back. It could say, "Look folks, we cannot honour our part of the agreement; therefore, we will at least give you back your money". If I sign a contract with somebody who does not perform his part of it, surely I am entitled to damages or at least to get my investment back. The government stopped that. There is no shame on the government benches, Mr. Speaker.
I have examined what happens with other nations because I was interested in the extent of centralization of power and socialism that there has to be before a system breaks down.
We all know that in Poland people have to stand in line to get food. Some people may think that this is because the government took over the farms, but that is not so; over 90 per cent of the farmland in Poland is owned by individuals. The government has taken over all the support services, however, such as the distribution of fertilizer and seeds as well as the processing of crops. So even if ownership of land is left in the hands of individuals, they will still have to stand in food lines if there has been nationalization of the infrastructure of farming. That is what happened in Poland.
We have an example of this in Canada that members of the New Democratic Party should be glad to-
