subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure for me to take part in the budget debate this afternoon. I would like to remind my colleagues that in the last few days, all the media have been saying that while the November budget was prepared by public servants, the latest budget was prepared by politicians. That reminds me of a saying that is rather popular in my area: The experts are always right except when things go wrong, and then we call in the politicians. Let me give you an example. In October 1981, I wrote to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to submit a proposal for a Canadian interest rate policy. I thought he might find it useful in preparing the November budget, but coming from a member and a politician-and since the budget was apparently prepared by public servants-obviously my proposal was not accepted.
July 8, 1982

It is some consolation to me today that the Minister of Finance probably decided, this time around, to put his hand in, and I see that the budget contains most of my recommendations. This is rather interesting because, at the time, I told him how important the interest rate issue was to Canadians, and I also told him about the uncertainty caused both by inflation and high interest rates, especially for farmers, the housing industry and small and medium-sized businesses. I tried to draft a policy statement, in very simple terms, that would deal with inflation and interest rates while at the same time protecting investor profits. I knew my concept could be further refined but, in any case, the important thing was to propose a truly Canadian policy on interest rates that would apply to very specific areas such as agriculture, housing and small and medium-sized businesses.
I therefore proposed a formula that dealt both with the rate of inflation and investor returns, and I told the minister that interest rates should never be in excess of 75 per cent of the market rate. I submitted a series of tables, and this is all in line with what the minister put into his budget. For instance, with an inflation rate of 3 per cent we have an interest rate of 9 per cent, and an inflation rate of 12 per cent could raise the interest rate to 18 per cent. The minister is proposing more or less the same thing, although with a different formula. And that is why this evening I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, with this opportunity to inform the House that the June 28 budget meets my expectations, especially in the areas I mentioned.
I should like to go over what the budget means to the average Canadian citizen. I believe that the budget is made for Canadians as a whole. It will help those who most need lower interest rates. Parents who have trouble making both ends meet will receive higher tax credits. Purchasers of new houses will receive a grant. Businesses will pay less to borrow from the banks. Of course, government tax revenues will be reallocated during the next two years to activities that will create jobs and promote investment immediately. This budget aims at restoring confidence, which was on the decline, as everyone agrees, confidence in a future when inflation will be lower and new investments will create the jobs needed. With this budget, the government is taking the lead in a two-year national effort. It wants to join with the other levels of government, businesses and workers to reduce inflation and promote economic recovery.
What are we doing exactly? Instead of letting wage settlements attempt to catch up with inflation, the government has decided to limit salary increases in the public service to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. What does this mean exactly? It means that the 500,000 people who work for the government and Crown corporations will get a maximum increase of 6 per cent. This will represent a saving of $250 million this year and $550 million next year for allocation to programs designed to stimulate the economy and create much
The Budget-Mr. Comtois
needed jobs. Who will be affected by this initiative? Everyone who works for the government and for most Crown corporations, ministers, Members of Parliament, Senators, deputy ministers and senior public servants, or about 500,000 people.
It is to be hoped that this decision will make provincial and municipal governments reflect on their own approach. Let us hope also that big companies, utility companies and labour unions will consider this suggestion carefully. If all sectors of society could agree voluntarily on a ceiling of 6 per cent, inflation would be reduced and more jobs would be created before long. What is the government trying to achieve in the June 28 budget? First, to tackle high interest rates-the highest priority, of course-at the same time to tackle inflation, to reallocate funds in order to create jobs, to help the housing industry and to introduce tax proposals. These are the five important points to remember. How does the budget tackle high interest rates? In order to promote the housing industry, the purchasers of new homes will receive a $3,000 grant on purchase. This is a positive measure since we know that housing is the prime industry to get the economy moving.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in my constituency of Terrebonne, contractors used to be able to build from 2,500 to 3,000 new homes a year. Last year, only 400 to 500 homes were built. This year, only a few hundred homes have been built to date. Thanks to this measure and others, it will be possible to boost residential construction without delay, and this will create thousands of jobs and generate economic benefits throughout Canada.
Second, small businesses will be able to secure loans at interest rates 4 percentage points lower than prevailing rates to invest in new plants and equipment. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this is very much like the proposals I submitted to the minister last year. Farmers will also be able to secure loans at interest rates 4 percentage points lower than prevailing rates to finance new equipment. As for fishermen, they will also be able to secure loans at lower interest rates to finance new equipment.
Another way of fighting high interest rates will be the creation of a new type of indexed term deposit certificate with a competitive interest rate. Income tax will be paid only on that part of interest income that exceeds the inflation rate, and here again I could give examples. If for instance a person bought a $1,000 indexed term deposit certificate with a 16 per cent interest rate while the inflation rate is 11 per cent, his or her interest income would be $160 but he or she would be taxed only on $50, the difference between the inflation rate and the interest rate. Again, it can be seen that these factors are taken into account, as I had suggested.
These new indexed term deposit certificates should attract $3 billion a year that will be available for reduced interest rate loans, through that tax relief, to new home buyers because the big problem for buyers is high interest rate and the unavailability of long-term loans. Currently, this is the real cause of the

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Comtois
slump in residential construction. When the proposed plan matures, small businesses, farmers and fishermen will be in a position to borrow some $12 billion to $15 billion a year at reduced interest rates, through that tax relief, to invest in new plants and equipment.
Second, while stimulating employment, residential construction, the expansion of small and medium businesses, farming and fishing, we must try to reduce inflation, and to that end, we have decided to place a 6 per cent ceiling on the indexation of deductions and personal income tax brackets for the 1983 tax year, and of 5 per cent for 1984. In order to set the example for provinces and private industry, the government is putting a limit on pay increases throughout the Civil Service. Mr. Speaker, it is my view that examples will be followed, and hopefully other sectors in this country will follow suit and fight inflation also. Therefore, these specific measures on public servants, salaries, transfer payments and administered prices show that the government is embarking on a two-year fight on inflation. This, in my view, is the message we must put across to our people.
There is also the $1.4 billion funding for direct job creation and other programs. Much criticism is being levelled at the government deficit that will total $19.6 billion. That criticism borders on obsession. If we can reduce our expenditures generally, instead of directly reducing the deficit, let us invest those expenditure reductions into the most dynamic areas. I feel there should be a review every two or three months, following which the most buoyant industries in our economy would receive more assistance in order to stimulate job creation while those which are lagging behind should of necessity receive less. This is the right way, in my view, to promote economic growth efficiently in this country. I believe that the best way to reduce the deficit is to generate higher revenues instead of cutting left and right through our often essential programs, in social services for instance. Therefore let us generate more economic activity, more revenues for the government, and the deficit will reduce itself, without making cuts that are too harsh for most Canadians. We should encourage competition between the most aggressive businessmen in this country. For this reason, I wholeheartedly support direct job-creation programs in some specific sectors. We have allotted, among others, $300 million to existing incentive programs to create employment in private industry. Two hundred million dollars more will be allotted to direct job-creation and $400 million to housing. As I said earlier, this plan can be very quickly and very easily carried out. Mr. Speaker, there are many builders in my area. Last week I met one who told me that in Canada we have all we need. We have concrete, steel, lumber, all kinds of materials and trained labour, nevertheless the construction industry is in trouble. Why is that? The problem is uncertainty, excessively high interest rates, inflation, the investor's reluctance to get involved in development programs and buyers' fear. But I
think that the steps included in the budget will succeed in restoring confidence, which is vital to economic recovery.
In addition, $400 million will be earmarked for the reduction of interests charged to small businessmen who are borrowing to make new investments in job creation and $100 million for the reduction of interests charged to farmers who are experiencing financial problems. I feel that it is an excellent measure. Our farmers need those funds to survive the recession.
Housing assistance is divided into five specific points. First, buyers of a new house, the construction of which started before December 31, 1982 will receive a $3,000 grant. Any first buyer of a house is eligible for the $3,000 grant. That is absolutely essential in our program. In addition, the Canada Home Renovation Program has been given an additional $30 million. Once again, such a program can easily be implemented.
To meet the special needs of low-income families, the NonProfit Housing Assistance will be increased from 25,000 to 27,500 units this year. There will also be more flexibility in the interest-free loans made available under the Canada Assisted Rental Program which has been experiencing some problems; but with more flexibility, I am sure the program will quickly receive a new impetus. Lastly, the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan is extended to December 31, 1983 and owners who have to pay more than 30 per cent of their gross income on their mortgage as a result of a mortgage renewal after the tabling of the budget will be eligible for a $3,000 grant. They will no longer have to defer their interests to become eligible.
In addition, tax proposals, if implemented, would allow Canadians who invest in a new form of term deposit to pay tax only on that part of the interest that exceeds the rate of inflation. The money could be channelled, at rates from 3 to 6 percentage points lower than prevailing rates, to buyers of new houses as well as to small businesses, farmers and fishermen who invest in new plants and equipment. A new registered investment plan is proposed providing for the purchase of publicly traded common shares of Canadian corporations. Half the capital gains would be taxable each year as in the past, but only to the extent where gains exceeds the rate of inflation.
So, Mr. Speaker, the public is invited to study those proposals and make their comments known as soon as possible. A committee of prominent financiers, accountants and economists has also been set up to look into the feasibility of the various proposals. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this advisory committee on inflation and the taxation of personal investments is to report at the latest next September 30.
I think we should insist that this committee table its report as soon as possible, on the 15th of August if at all possible, to do away with the uncertainty that will once again exist about this new program during coming weeks. I am sure the committee could meet every day, if need be, for two or three weeks, then report on August 15, so that the government and the



July 8, 1982

Minister of Finance can announce their decisions with regard to the new program that will be implemented.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to keep my hon. colleagues any longer. In closing I should like to say that Canadians expected the Minister of Finance to take rather drastic measures. All in all, this budget meets their hopes. I am convinced that if each and every Canadian wants to co-operate by lowering his or her expectations, we can not only get the economy back on track but also reduce our deficit, create thousands of jobs and once again give our fellow-citizens all the services they can rightly expect. In a society such as ours, a society built on sharing, which is what Canada is, to be shared goods must first be generated. I believe the budget sets us on the right track. I am convinced its effects will soon start to be felt and that as early as next September and October, statistics and reports will tell that the budget has achieved its goal allowing the economy to gather steam for a major recovery.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget we got from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) last November deepened the recession that this country was experiencing at that time. The budget we got a few days ago from the same Minister of Finance guarantees that we will have a continuing and an even more serious recession to come.
When the minister delivered his budget last November we had 891,000 people unemployed, which represented 7.5 per cent of the labour force. He forecast then that in 1982 we would have 946,000 people or 7.8 per cent of the labour force unemployed. Instead, when he presented his budget a few days ago, we had 1,241,000 people or 10.4 per cent of the labour force unemployed. Members of Parliament know that the figure of 1,241,000 does not reflect accurately the number of unemployed. Members of Parliament know that there are in many parts of this country tens of thousands, indeed, hundreds of thousands of Canadians who have given up looking for work. They have given up looking because in their one-industry towns there simply is no work, we not only have 10.4 per cent of our labour force unemployed but we have almost double that percentage of our young people who are unemployed. A whole generation of young Canadians, the best educated and the best trained that we have ever produced, are being consigned to the scrap heap by the mistaken policies of the government.
When the Minister of Finance delivered his budget last November the cost of living was rising at 12.7 per cent per year. When he delivered his most recent budget, the cost of living was 11.8 per cent and is still rising. Wages are rising by 11.2 per cent. In other words, wages are rising by less than the increase in the cost of living. That situation has been going on for five years. The real income of ordinary Canadians has gone down, yet we are told by the government that the way to stop inflation is to cap by law the wages of public servants. The government hopes that other employers in the public and private sector will follow suit despite the fact that real earnings, the real living standard of ordinary Canadians, has gone
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
down in recent years rather than up. To blame ordinary Canadians for inflation is patent nonsense.
Business bankruptcies were running at 642 a month last November at the time when the Minister of Finance presented his budget. Business bankruptcies are now running at 886 a month. That is an increase of 38 per cent, and it is continuing to increase.
We are told that the deficit which the Minister of Finance estimated would be $10 billion last November is now estimated to be $19 million. We should ask ourselves, and the minister should ask himself, why the deficit has almost doubled in a period of just a few months. The reasons are not very difficult to find. It is not because of poor management, although there is poor management according to members of the official opposition. The deficit is up because of the recession we are in, because of the 1.25 million people who are unemployed, who by virtue of not working are not paying income tax and are not purchasing the goods and services which they need and on which they would be paying sales tax. Companies are not making profits, therefore they are not paying the amount of corporation tax they used to pay. Government revenues are way down. At the same time that government revenues are way down, expenditures are rising. Of course, they are rising because if you have more people unemployed than ever before unemployment insurance benefits will escalate. Unemployment insurance benefits are up over 40 per cent, I believe, over last year. When the unemployed run out of unemployment insurance benefits they go on welfare, and costs to the federal government, the provinces and municipalities go up. Of course, the deficit is up.
I predict that in the fall we will get another borrowing bill which will be even bigger than the one we are going to have to deal with in the next week or so. Last November when the Minister of Finance presented his then budget, manufacturing capacity utilization was running at over 73 per cent. In other words, Canadian plants were running at over 73 per cent of their ability to produce. When the minister presented his budget a few days ago plant capacity was running at less than 70 per cent. Obviously, when plants are running at less than 70 per cent capacity what is needed to get them working at a higher capacity and what is needed to get Canadians back to work is to increase the purchasing power of Canadians. If the people had more purchasing power they could buy the goods and services they need produced by other Canadians. As a result there would be a reduction in the number of people unemployed. But instead of following policies which would increase the ability of Canadians to buy the goods and services we can produce, ordinary Canadians get a tax increase. The partial deindexation of income tax would take $1.3 billion, that is $1,300 million, out of the pockets of Canadians. If you add wage controls in the public sector, about which I will speak later, and the partial deindexation of family allowances and pensions, you add another $1.3 billion which the government proposes to take out of the pockets of Canadians in the next 20 months.
July 8, 1982

The Budget-Mr. Orlilcow
That is the wrong policy to follow if we want to get people back to work.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
