subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments in which I spoke before the supper break I made the point that as a result of the deindexing of income taxes, of the capping of the indexation of pensions and of the restraint put on public service wages and salaries, Canadians will have a reduction in their take-home income in the next two years of $2.6 billion. However, not all Canadians will suffer as a result of the last two budgets brought forward by the present Minister of Finance. The people at the top will pay substantially less in income tax than they paid before last November's budget because of the sharp reduction in their marginal tax rate which the Minister of Finance put into effect; it was reduced from over 60 per cent to 50 per cent.
According to this week's edition of The Financial Post, a taxpayer with a wife and two children and a taxable income of $20,000 would have paid, before last November's budget, $2,502 in income tax. After the November budget and after the budget of a few days ago, he will have to pay $2,434, a reduction of less than $100. Before last November's budget, the taxpayer with a $200,000 income would have paid $98,000 in income tax. After the November budget that tax would have been reduced to $87,276. After this last budget it was increased to $87,860. Therefore, the taxpayer with an income of $200,000 received a reduction of over $10,000. That is typical of the Liberals, "To those who have shall be given".
I would like to make a few remarks about what the government is doing to our old age pensioners. I say this with great regret because we in our party had great respect for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). We applauded the speeches she made all across Canada when she talked about the tens of thousands of pensioners, particularly women pensioners, who are living on old age pensions and GIS. She pointed out that many of them live in poverty. Now she has caved in and given up the fight. She has agreed to the disastrous decision of the Minister of Finance.
We should study what will happen to our pensioners and consider for a few moments the history of pensions in Canada. It has taken generations to develop pension plans. I believe our first pension plans began in 1926. It has taken all these years to lay the foundation for a pension system which would permit our retired people to live in some dignity and comfort. In 1926
we started with a pension of $20 a month for people 70 years old. In order to receive that pension they had to pass a means test. Gradually over the years the age for pension eligibility was reduced.
A few years ago indexing was introduced. I know that our Conservative friends did not like indexing and thought it was detrimental. But where would our pensioners be now if indexing was not implemented during what the Conservatives felt was the terrible minority Parliament of 1972 and 1973? At the present time, pensioners who receive old age security benefits receive $239 a month. Until the capping of indexation in last week's budget they were receiving the full indexation. The cost of living will rise by more than 11 per cent this year. The government has indicated that old age pensioners will receive an increase of only 6 per cent in the coming year, regardless of what rise occurs in the cost of living, and they will receive 5 per cent the following year, regardless of how much the cost of living will go up for that year. If the quarterly increases in 1983 for old age pensioners with full indexation was worked out at an annual rate of 10 per cent-we must remember that we have inflation of 11.5 per cent-rather than cap it at 6 per cent, at which it is now, the loss will be $77 in the next year, rather than the $55 the minister is talking about. But in the second year, with a 5 per cent ceiling on old age security payments, the real loss will be $218. Therefore, over the next two years, old age security pensioners will lose approximately $300, or $12 a month.
However, this is not the most serious effect. The fact is that if full indexing starts two years from now-one must ask oneself if we will ever see full indexing again once it has been taken away-but if full indexing starts in 1984, it will start at the lower amount. The pensioners will never catch up to what they would have received if indexation had not been capped as is proposed by the minister.
If we had the actuaries calculate the loss to pensioners over their whole lives-as I say, they will never make up that $300 which is to be taken away from them by the government in the next two years-I have been told that over the whole of their lives they will be shortchanged by several billion dollars. In view of the views which the Minister of National Health and Welfare has expressed so frequently, she should never have accepted this. I suggest that she should have resigned rather than accept it.
The government has put a 6 per cent limit on increases permitted to public servants in the coming year. The government implies that they will not lose too much because the cost of living will be brought down to 6 per cent. There is no evidence that can be given by the government that the 11 per cent cost of living today can be reduced to 6 per cent. The government cannot reduce the cost of living because it continues to follow the monetarist policy of high interest, antiintervention, anti-full employment and anti-demand and management policies which have been endorsed by this government for many years and unfortunately endorsed by the short-
July 8, 1982

lived Conservative government. That government kept following the same course. It retained the same head of the Bank of Canada and brought in a deputy minister whose views must be similar to those of the Liberals since he is one of the so-called experts on that team which advises the Minister of Finance.
There will be no substantial decrease in interest rates. The budget does nothing to end the strangulation of the economy which has been caused by high interest rates. This is due to the government's insisting on following the advice of the Bank of Canada in tying our dollar to the American dollar. We must keep in mind that, on the advice of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the government made desperate efforts to keep the dollar at 85 cents U.S. When that did not work it made strenuous efforts to keep the dollar at 80 cents U.S. Now it is making the same kind of efforts-probably just as futile-to keep the dollar above 75 cents, U.S.
In order to do this, interest rates for Canadians have to be kept high. Therefore, individual Canadians such as farmers, home owners and small-business men now have to pay interest rates at 20 per cent or higher. Farmers, businessmen and home owners have repeatedly told the government and other members when they appeared before the finance committee which was looking into bank profits that they cannot live with interest rates which are 20 per cent or more.
Bankruptcies are at an all time high. Farmers are going out of production. Home construction is now at an all-time low. There are less than 120,000 units per year being built. This is half of the number of units being built a few years ago.
Given the interest rates which we have today there can be little, if any, reduction in the cost of living. How can interest rates be lowered and how can people be encouraged to invest in productive ways when they can do so much better by simply depositing their money in the bank or purchasing Canada Savings Bonds? Although many companies need to be modernized, expanded or computerized, what Canadian who has some savings will invest his money in the stocks of some company or buy long-term bonds when he can get 14 per cent or 15 per cent from term deposits? A year ago Canadians were able to get 19.5 per cent interest on Canada savings bonds. The result is that investment in Canadian companies has dried up. We now see Canadian companies which used to be able to sell shares or long term bonds being forced to go to the banks to borrow hundreds of millions of dollars, indeed billions of dollars, from the bank on short-term loans.
A couple of weeks ago The Financial Post listed approximately 15 of the largest companies in Canada which are paying anywhere from 75 per cent to 150 per cent of their entire cash flow in interest payments. Those companies are hanging on for dear life. Many of those companies would now be bankrupt if it were not for the banks carrying them.
Let me give hon. members another reason that it is ridiculous to talk about bringing the rate of inflation down to 6 per cent. The government said that it could not honour the contracts which it had signed with its employees in good faith, which gave the employees more than 6 per cent in wage and
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
salary increases. It must bring in special legislation to restrict wage and salary increases to 6 per cent in the coming year and to 5 per cent the next, but the Government of Canada made an agreement with the producing provinces about the price of oil. On July 1, a few days ago, the price of a barrel of oil went up $2.25. On January 1 of 1983 it will go up $4 a barrel, and on July 1, 1983 it will go up another $4 a barrel. That is $10.25 in one year. Every increase of a dollar in the price of a barrel of oil adds half a percentage point to the cost of living. So, when we are speaking of a $10 increase in the price of a barrel of oil, we are looking at a 5 per cent increase in the cost of living in the next year, just because of the increased cost of energy. When the leader of our party suggested to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that he should go to the producing provinces and ask them to give up some or all of that price increase to help keep the cost of living from rising, the Prime Minister said, "We have an agreement. We cannot vary it". So it obviously depends upon whom one has the agreement with. An agreement with our employees can be ignored, can be overruled, however, can that be done with an agreement with the producing provinces or the oil companies? It cannot be done.
Let us look for a moment at the limits put on the salaries of public servants. The government will limit them to 6 per cent in the coming year and to 5 per cent in the following year. As I have said, the cost of living will go up much more than 6 per cent. I have a friend who likes to do some modest wagering, and he has asked me to ask Liberal Members of Parliament who really believe the government will get the rate of inflation down to 6 per cent to contact me. He will cover all the money they would like to bet that the cost of living will come down by that amount. But let us look at what 6 per cent limit means. For the civil servant who is making $90,000, of whom there are some, it means an increase of between $5,000 and $6,000, but for the hundreds of thousands who make between $11,000 and $12,000 it means an increase limited to between $600 and $700. That is the Liberal idea of equity.
We are told that this budget will help create new jobs. Keep in mind that we have over 1.25 million unemployed. So what does the government propose in the way of job creation? It will give a $3,000 grant to purchasers of new homes under certain conditions, but it has put a limit of $300 million on the amount of money allocated for that purpose. The government itself estimates that this will provide 50,000 jobs in two years; in other words, 25,000 jobs will be created in each of the two years. The $3,000 grant can, of course, be passed along in the form of higher prices, and we have already seen some evidence that that is happening.
The problem of the prospective home purchasers is not, and has never really been, his inability to make the downpayment. The problem of the home purchaser is that he cannot afford the monthly mortgage payments with the present interest rates of 20 per cent or more. Therefore, the incomes of 90 per cent of Canadians are below what is necessary to be able to afford a house. We have the home renovation plan to which $30 million has been allocated. Again, it is hoped that it will create 10,000 jobs in the next two years.

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not a chance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then we have the Canada mortgage renewal plan which makes it possible for people who formerly qualified only for interest deferrals to get grants now of up to $3,000 or whatever is required to keep their mortgage payments at 30 per cent of their gross income. That will not help much because only $25 million to $50 million has been allocated to the program. When that money runs out, they will be back in the same box they were before, as they will not be able to afford the monthly payments. Then, of course, we heard the announcement by the minister in charge of housing that we will have 2,500 more non-profit or co-operative housing units. That will not meet the need in one of the big cities in Canada, let alone all across the country. All together, if ail these housing proposals work, and that is very doubtful, we will provide 57,000 jobs in the next year and 61,000 in the following year.
What are the other job-creation programs proposed by the government? The Canada community development projects have been allocated $200 million, which will provide 23,000 jobs this year and 23,000 jobs next year. Then $300 million is supposedly to be allocated for economic development initiatives. We have heard this song before.
Let us look at one which is supposed to be a jewel in the government's arsenal, the ILAP program, announced a year and a half ago, to which $350 million was allocated. It was set up supposedly to help those communities devastated by layoffs and initiate economic resurgence. In a year and a half, less than 10 per cent of the $350 million allocated to this program has been used and only 10 per cent of the workers in some of the designated communities, which were supposed to benefit from the adjustment measures, are eligible.
Let us look at the total package the government is proposing. All of its programs together will provide 80,000 jobs this year and 84,500 jobs next year. That comes at a time when we have more than 1.25 million unemployed. What we need are real programs to put people back to work, not temporary jobs. We have 165,000 unemployed construction workers, sitting at home drawing unemployment insurance, when they want to be out working. We need a real housing program. We need to set ourselves the objective of doubling the number of houses we are building right now and building 225,000 homes in the next year. But to do this, the government would have to allocate the money or tell the banks to set aside from their investment portfolios the money required, the $2 billion required for this kind of program, at interest rates which the Canadian people can afford to pay, and that is not 20 per cent plus.
The government and the experts have spoken about the tremendous increase in our exports: 50 per cent more wheat, 100 per cent more potash and 350 per cent more coal. Our transportation system barely meets its present shipments. We need to modernize the system. We need to double track, a promise the Prime Minister has forgotten. We need to bring the signal system into the twentieth century. We will not be able to achieve those objectives we discussed because our transportation system cannot do it. We need to start now, but
the railways, instead of hiring new people and buying new equipment, have major lay-offs. The government needs to be serious. It needs to deal with unemployment as the first objective on which it will go to work. It needs to stop conning the Canadian people that this program or any other program it has enunciated will really bring down the cost of living. That will not happen, and I think hon. members on the government side know it; but, of course, they cannot afford to admit it because they cannot take the political consequences. Therefore, we say to the government, be serious. Do the things which need to be done. The people in this country want to work. We have the manpower and the natural resources. We can put the people of Canada to work at meaningful jobs if we have the desire.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa Centre.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just turn off the mike!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a contribution to this debate on the budget, if the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) would pipe down. I will get to him in a minute.
I would like to talk about the budget, the thrust of the budget, what it does, what we are attempting to do with it and why I think it is the appropriate budget for the times, one that will set us on the track back to recovery.
The budget was intended to do a number of things. First, it was intended to intensify the anti-inflation fight. I just heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) say that we should effectively forget all other economic goals except unemployment. That just will not work. How are you going to get unemployment down? You will not beat the unemployment problem if you give up on the fight against inflation.
The hon. member talked about investment. He said that we need to have more investment. Why in the world would any Canadian invest money in this country with the kind of uncertainty that would be facing us if we allowed inflation to run to 20 per cent or 30 per cent? Countries that have followed a strategy such as the one outlined by that hon. member for Winnipeg North have reaped the whirlwind. They have had declining investment, declining growth and a declining standard of living. That policy is a bankrupt policy by a bankrupt party.
The budget was intended to intensify the fight against inflation, to bring inflation down to 6 per cent, to give a positive target as to where this government believes we can bring inflation over the next year. I think we can do it, but it will take the co-operation of all parties in our economic system. The government put forward a program that shows the leadership from the government sector. We are asking the provincial governments, the provincial public sectors, to join with us.
July 8, 1982

The federal government has put forward a program. Federal public servants, federal Crown corporations, federal regulated agencies as well as parliamentarians and senators will participate in that program. We are asking the provinces and municipalities to join with us. The public sector can show leadership. The people of Canada want leadership. They want to see action. This government has put forward a program which indicates that leadership. We are intensifying the fight against inflation. We are bringing forward more meaningful policies.
The second purpose of the budget is to try to restore some confidence, to put forward some programs that will lead to enhanced savings and investment in this country. If we are going to have increased productivity and an increased standard of living, we need to have increased investment. In order to have increased investment, we need increased savings.
There have been some innovative and creative proposals put forward that will be dealt with early in the fall when the House reconvenes and the committee reports back with regard to those programs for indexation of certain investment incomes.
Those are innovative ideas that are being well received by the investment community. The community indicates that when implemented, they will have a high chance of success. In addition, we have a program of restraint, a program to try to improve the investment climate so that we will have growth and development.
At the same time we have programs that were brought forward in the budget for specific assistance to those in greatest need. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the Speech from the Throne in 1980 indicated that one of the prime motivating forces underlying this government's policy would be to provide aid and assistance to those in greatest need. We are running a very large deficit. There can be no doubt about that. I will come to a more complete discussion of the deficit shortly.
With that situation facing us and the very real need for assistance to those suffering the greatest losses during this period of recession, moneys had to be freed elsewhere. That is the reason for the restraint program in the public sector. That is the reason for freeing funds from sources available to us in order to provide assistance.
That assistance is being provided by some $450 million in direct employment programs and $300 million in economic development assistance. The hon. member for Winnipeg North talked about the area of housing. I gained the impression that he thought these programs are frivolous. Last night the housing industry indicated that the housing package put forward in this budget will create upward of 65,000 new homes in Canada this year alone.
On the average, for every home built two to two and a half man-years of employment are created. Therefore, if you build 65,000 new homes, you create 130,000 to 150,000 jobs. Those are jobs in the area of home building. The housing industry, which will have to take the risks in building those new houses, has assessed those programs as being effective, having great potential for success, saying they will stimulate home building,
The Budget-Mr. Evans
home purchases by first-time buyers and the real estate and building sectors.
The other major area of assistance is the interest rate assistance, an increase of some $400 million to small businesses and some $200 million increase for farmers. Those are the basic areas to intensify the anti-inflation fight through pay restraints, changes to the indexing system and restrictions for the areas of administered pricing that fall within federal jurisdiction, through the program of restraint, 6 per cent restraint next year, and 5 per cent the year after. Through that program funds will be freed to be used to help those in greatest need in this country.
That is the Liberal tradition of sharing. That is the principle by which this government operates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You share with yourselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member says we share with ourselves. Sharing has been traditional in this country. Canadians have shared in times of difficulty. We are in a difficult period. The government is saying that if we share, the burden can be spread broadly. No one will have to give up much. As the burden is spread broadly, it will ensure that no individual suffers extreme damage during this period.
We heard a great deal of discussion about the deficit. We should look at what the increase is in the deficit and how it was caused. Is it, as some members opposite have said, an increase in government expenditure, an increase in program expenditures, a permanent increase in the level of the federal deficit? I will answer unequivocally, no, it is not.
Successive governments in the past have put in place programs to protect those in greatest need of assistance. From the forties to the fifties to the sixties, with the great depression in their memories, they have put in place programs so that when times are tough, those who are hardest hit by the economic downturns are cushioned. Liberal and Conservative governments of the sixties-primarily Liberal governments-put in place programs to ensure that there would be a social safety net under Canadians. That is the source of the increase in the deficit. When we go into an economic downturn, these automatic stabilizers, as they are called-expenditures for unemployment insurance, for social assistance, for the Canada Assistance Plan and expenses of that kind-increase automatically because more people are out of work. Those expenditures indeed increase. At the same time as the economy goes into a recession the revenues of the government drop. Tax revenues drop because profits go down. Fewer people are working and, as a result, tax revenues fall.
Let us look at those factors alone. The budget deficit in the 1981 budget was forecast to be $10.5 billion and the financial requirements were to be $6.6 billion. We have heard that the government is a terrible forecaster. I defy anyone in this House to bring forward a forecast made in October or November of 1981 which shows numbers different from those forecast by

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Evans
the Department of Finance at that time. There were none because no one, not in this country or in any other country, had any notion that the western economic world would go into the deep and prolonged recession we have gone into. The numbers were $10.5 billion for the deficit and $6.6 billion for financial requirements.
Let us look at what happened to revenues. Revenues declined because of the recession. Expenditures increased because of the automatic stabilizers, which transferred money to people in greatest need. The deficit is up to $19.6 billion because tax revenues have been reduced by $6.5 billion as a direct result of the recession. Because of automatic stabilizers expenditures have increased $2.5 billion. If we put those together, we find the explanation for the difference between the deficit forecast in November and the deficit we forecast for this year. It is not a matter of an increase in permanent program expenditures which would cause a permanent increase in the deficit. Indeed, if we do not consider interest payments on the debt as a part of this, we find that program expenditures by this government are forecast to increase this year by 10.7 per cent, which is less than the current rate of inflation. That has been the case in the past. Program expenditures over which government have direct control have increased by less than the rate of inflation over the last three or four years. There has indeed been restraint. However, as a result of rapidly rising interest rates, because of the automatic stabilizers and as a result of the decline in output and productivity-and therefore tax revenue-we have had what I would call-and I think I am correct in this-a temporary increase in the deficit during this period of recession. As we come out of this period of recession and go back to a period of restored growth, tax revenues will flow back in, people will be going back to work, payments by the Unemployment Insurance Commission will decline automatic stabilizer payments will diminish, revenues will increase and the temporary increase in the deficit will be eliminated.
I contrast this with the situation in the United States, because it is different. The United States deficit is not a temporary deficit. It is a forecast deficit which will increase year after year. We are talking about perhaps $145 billion this year and perhaps $200 billion the year after. That deficit is the direct result of increases in program expenditures by the Reagan administration and especially increases in defence expenditures and direct tax cuts. Those two programs will mean that the deficit in the United States will be a chronic deficit. It will not disappear as the U.S. economy comes out of recession. Indeed, it will continue to grow.
There is a very large difference between the deficit situation in Canada and that in the United States. One is an increase in the deficit caused by increases in permanent program expenditures-structural changes in the expenditure patterns of the government-and the Canadian situation is a temporary increase in the deficit caused by a reduction in revenues due to the recession and increases in automatic stabilizer payments caused, again, by the recession. That is the difference.
We are very concerned about our deficit. There is no way anyone could be anything but concerned about the deficit, unless he was a New Democrat. New Democrats really do not care at all about deficits. We have to be concerned, but I think we also have to understand what we are talking about. We must understand the nature of our deficit and why our country can handle it. We must understand why our capital markets can handle the kind of deficit situation we are facing.
I would like to talk about the restraint program because it is a very important aspect of the policy of the government. It is especially important to the people in my riding. There are two aspects of the restraint program. The first is the restraint of wages and salaries of public servants, Members of Parliament and Crown corporation employees as well as the control of administered prices to the levels of 6 per cent and 5 per cent. 1 support that. There is another aspect of the program, and that is deindexation. 1 support certain elements of that deindexation as well, but there is one element of deindexation about which I have serious questions. I intend to pursue those questions. I know you intend to pursue them as well, Mr. Speaker. The element to which I refer is the element of deindexation of public service superannuation. The reason I have questions about that is that contractual payments are made to individuals who made contributions during their working lives to fund indexation. If it could be shown that the fund which has been built up by public servants to fund the indexation of their pensions is inadequate or insufficient, then I could see justification for saying, "Yes, restraint". I have not seen that evidence. I have not seen anyone put forward evidence or indicate to me that there is evidence which indicates that the funding of that indexation program is inadequate. I will have to see that evidence before I can support this particular element of the deindexation program. If public servants in our ridings, Mr. Speaker, and all across the country made contributions to that fund which are adequate to cover the indexation of their superannuation payments, then I do not think that should be part of the restraint program.
I do support the over-all restraint program, but I put forward the caveat that I do intend to pursue that one element of the program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The one that affects your riding.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the government had to show leadership. Public servants, ourselves and employees of Crown corporations are all employees of the people. We work for the taxpayer, and if the taxpayer is suffering under an increasing burden and if the taxpayer is suffering as a result of the recession, it certainly seems to me to be fair and equitable that the employees of those taxpayers should be willing to share some of that burden. The request is not for a large sharing. We are not saying jobs will be eliminated or that people will be thrown out onto the streets. Indeed, there is job security in the public service. Instead of full indexation of the salaries of public servants, Members of Parliament and Crown corporation employees, we are saying there will be increases, but the increase in the first year will be limited to 6 per cent and in the
July 8, 1982

second year to 5 per cent. After all, if we are successful and bring inflation down to 6 per cent, there will be no suffering by anyone as a result of that program. Even if we do not succeed in bringing inflation down to 6 per cent, I think it is only fair that those of us who work for the people of this country share the burden they carry. It is only fair, when 1.2 million people in the private sector are unemployed, that those of us in the public sector paid by the private sector, share, and that we free money to put those people back to gainful employment.
I find nothing wrong with asking that the public sector, the employees of the people, share the burden. 1 think it is totally sensible, equitable and honest for the public sector at the federal, provincial and municipal level to share the burden carried by the private sector. I think it is fair and equitable and I support that request.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You would!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hear the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) indicating that this is a terrible thing. It was not this government that proposed to cut 60,000 jobs from the public service; it was the government of the party opposite that proposed to cut 20,000 jobs a year. It was not a matter of asking for restraint in wage demands with job security; it was a matter of eliminating 60,000 jobs. One out of every five jobs in the federal public service would have gone. Today it is not just a matter of restraint, it is not a matter of having a job at all. The hypocrisy of hon. members opposite is totally incredible, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) accept a question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will when I complete my remarks, Mr. Speaker.
I think that the program must be national in scope. The Prime Minister made an extremely important point in question period just the other day and-and I am not talking out of place here-in caucus as well. He indicated that we are going to try to achieve that national restraint in a Liberal way; that is, voluntarily. We will show leadership at the federal level and we will ask for restraint in the private sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now members of the NDP are getting up on their hind legs. They talk about restraint in the private sector, restraint on business firms, restraint on bank profits and restraint on private sector profits, but what about restraint on union demands? We do not hear about that. We hear about restraint on everything else but not on union demands because the CLC funds the NDP.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You are showing your true colours now.
The Budget-Mr. Evans

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think we must have restraint at all levels; the public sector and the private sector.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are union bashing now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not union bashing. That is not what I am saying at all. Restraint is being imposed on all parts of the private sector. Just tonight we heard that corporate profits declined by 44 per cent in the first quarter of this year and by 51 per cent over the last year. That is restraint. That is imposing a burden on the private sector. We have heard that time and time again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that voluntary?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: White collar workers and management are taking 10 and 15 per cent cuts in their salaries.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that voluntary?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they are voluntary cuts in salaries. I wonder if there was restraint in the demands made by Mr. McDermott and his colleagues in the union leadership when the INCO workers were put out of jobs? I did not hear about any restraint there. I think it is important that we look at the situation in the labour market if Canada is to restore prosperity and growth. If we are to have an increase in employment-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You guys would have to resign.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-we must have restraint in wage demands because they impose costs on business firms that cannot be passed on. As a result, profits are down by 44 per cent in the first quarter of this year and 51 per cent over last year. That corporate profit burden must be shared by owners and workers alike if this country is to see renewed growth, an increase in productivity and an increase in the number of jobs.
It is fine for workers or for leaders of the union movement to say that they will not give concessions. As they are saying that, the membership of their unions is becoming smaller and smaller. The people on the edges are being thrown out of work. Does that sound fair and equitable? It is not in the interests of the workers.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the prices charged by regulated industries. We have a regulated sector in this country. Bell Canada, for instance, is asking for a rather substantial increase in rates; Consumers Gas is asking for a rather substantial increase in rates, and so is Ontario Hydro. I do not think that can be allowed. Firms in the private sector are facing a decline in demand for their goods and thus, a massive decline in profitability. They are unable to raise prices and indeed, in some cases, prices have been falling. But in the regulated sector prices have been increasing in the last two years by about 18 per cent per year when inflation was running at 11 or 12 per cent. That means that the private sector price increases were going up far less than 12 per cent. That is not fair, Mr. Speaker. The regulated sector has been granted virtual monopolies on various services because they are essential in the public interest.

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
We cannot have one sector of the economy operating on a cost plus basis. No matter what the cost increases are, they go to the CTC or the CRCT and say that costs have increased and therefore they must have an increase in price. That must not occur in the regulated sector because it does not occur in the unregulated sector, the private sector. What is fair for the unregulated sector must be imposed on the regulated sector. The 6 and 5 per cent must be imposed on the regulated sector not only at the federal level but also on the regulated industries at the provincial level. They must operate under the same conditions as the private sector.
It is not fair to ask the unregulated private sector employees to suffer unemployment and suffer bankruptcies when the public sector and the regulated sector go on imposing ever higher costs on the people of the country. We must restrain ourselves.
The government has introduced a program to spread the burden equitably and ensure that all of us share it. By doing so we will bring inflation down and set the stage for renewed economic growth in the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a very short question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly, Mr. Speaker. He is harmless.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) had a couple of children old enough to buy a new home today, would he advise them to buy a new house at present interest rates, even with the grants the government proposes to give?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would advise my children to buy homes because I have great faith in the future of this country. I know we are going to recover and it is going to be a good buy for them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The time of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre has been exhausted.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has exhausted our patience!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Grey-Simcoe.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this budget debate. The hon. member who just spoke has shown by the desperate tone of his voice and his delivery that he is not quite sure whether he believes in what he was saying but desperately wants us to believe him. It reminds me of the story, Mr. Speaker, of the church janitor whose job it was to clean up after the minister had finished his sermon and the congregation had left. When the janitor approached the pulpit he came across the minister's sermon notes which the minister had forgotten. He observed
that the minister had bracketed a couple of paragraphs and noted this on the side of the page: "Argument weak here. Shout like hell". I believe that is what the hon. member was trying to do to us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression that, because the November budget proved to be such a nonsensical fiasco, this new budget would have indicated that the government did indeed see the error of its ways and consequently would bring forth a budget which would have indeed clearly focused itself on the myriad problems facing all Canadians, that it would come forth with the needed solutions to help negate the anxiety and unemployment in the country, our gloomy economy and, above all, effectively reduce interest rates which are causing such great havoc, untold misery and fear among all Canadians, including the business, agricultural and industrial areas of our country.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, utterly fails to address itself to the real problems facing our country. It shows that the government has learned very little indeed since the November 12 budget. Nothing has been done to bring down the interest rates which are slowly but surely squeezing the life out of our economy and destroying the hopes and dreams of millions of Canadians. How high interest rates will go is anyone's guess. Neither the government nor the Bank of Canada have shown leadership in this regard. As far as I can see they are both floating as badly as our dollar, which is now facing an unprecedented devaluation, and which in turn has dumped Canada from the position of the third highest standard of living to fifteenth. The state of being low man on the totem pole has been exacerbated as well by our very high budget deficit of some S20 billion and our million-plus unemployment.
These are the real causes of our problems, Mr. Speaker, but the government, instead of directly addressing itself to those causes, is content to treat the symptoms with band-aid medication-nothing but short-term band-aid policies-hoping against hope that the economy might, just might have an upswing so that it can be bailed out. Better still, the government hopes that the American economy will improve so that it can snatch at the Americans' coattails like a drowning man going down for the third time, grasping wildly at anything to save himself.
Canadians are being told that this budget is one of restraint. How gullible does this government think Canadians are? How can a government ask for restraint from taxpayers when it refuses to get its own house in order? How can people be expected to show restraint when this budget will increase government spending by some 20 per cent and double the size of the deficit compared to last November? It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the government does not intend to practise what it preaches. There is no question that Canadians are still in shock over the large deficit. Not only that, the bottom line of the budget indicates quite clearly that the government has
July 8, 1982

totally abdicated responsibility in carrying out its mandate to govern.
The budget, Mr. Speaker, has been described as a flog, a dud, a wet blanket thrown over a dying patient. One businessman put it this way: "We have been holding on by the skin of our teeth waiting for Ottawa to do something, and now this. In another few months it won't matter any more. We will all be done like our over-cooked dinner." There is no question that since 1970 federal governments have borrowed their way to the very brink of disaster, and that the dam on federal spending has finally burst. Government debt as of the 1982-83 fiscal year will amount of $132 billion. Twenty-five per cent of the 1982-83 budget of $78 billion will be needed just to pay interest on the national debt. Behind all this borrowing, there has been an unlimited growth in the size of the government. To be fair, this also reflects the growth of provincial and municipal governments. That is why Canada is mired in the depths of high interest rates and a deep recession. The Bank of Canada's decision to restrict the money supply should have had the effect of bringing interest rates down, but as long as it refuses to reduce the deficit and continues to borrow, we will have high interest rates and high inflation. As long as governments compete with private enterprise for the limited supply of investment capital, there will not be economic renewal.
Massive government borrowing has put tremendous pressure on the money markets, Mr. Speaker, which only increases interest rates. The government's cash requirement this year is over $17 billion, which makes it the largest single competitor for the limited dollars in the money markets. Given this situation, no wonder interest rates are going up and up. The irony is that although this budget will raise an additional $1.3 billion in revenue, none of it will be spent to reduce the deficit. Nothing this government has done has convinced the international money markets that it is serious about reducing the deficit.
The saddest part of the budget, Mr. Speaker, is that the government has singled out those Canadians who are on spouses' allowance, disability pensions and old age pensions to help pay for its mistakes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely shameful.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is asking those Canadians who paid their dues, and who now deserve support, to shoulder the burden by deindexing their pensions to 6 per cent. Their pensions are no longer inflation-proof, so their income will now dwindle away. Also distressing is the deindexing of personal income tax, which is nothing short of an under the table tax increase of $1.3 billion. As we all know, by doing this the government is admitting that it has a vested interest in inflation because as incomes increase due to inflation, tax revenues rise. For this reason alone, any attempt to deindex should be condemned outright and withdrawn.
One of the most nagging concerns of the Canadian business world, Mr. Speaker, is the government's apparent indifference to foreign investment. It is doing practically everything it can to discourage foreign investment in our country, investment which is badly needed to reawaken our slumbering economy
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
and get us back on track again. The result is that we are seen by other countries as presenting a schizophrenic image in our negative attitude to foreign investment. The Foreign Investment Review Agency is of great concern to foreign investors. Despite eight years of operation there is still no clear understanding of what is meant by the term "significant benefit to Canada". Foreign investors still do not know what the ground rules of FIRA are. When it was set up it was originally intended that 60 days would be a sufficient period for the examination of a proposal, and that extensions would only be used in extraordinary circumstances. However, at the present time over 50 per cent of applications to FIRA take more than five months before they receive a definite answer. The lack of clarity and the long waiting period, do nothing but create an unhealthy element of uncertainty that distracts foreign investors. The bottom line on Canada's treatment of foreign investment is that we are being perceived as an inhospitable place in which to invest. Such an image once entrenched is not easy to change and would be very harmful to our long-term interests.
1 would like to turn for a moment to the Canadian dollar. The breaking of the Canadian dollar to below its 1931 level brought forth the usual government excuse, the strength of the American dollar. The strength of the U.S. dollar is just a convenient whipping boy for the government. The real problem goes much deeper. Canada's inflation rate is higher than the U.S. rate because the government has done practically nothing to reduce its deficits, thereby leading to "counterfeiting" more money each year. Government deficits and out-of-line union demands have eroded our dollar since the 1970s. But now we have a new force to reckon with which threatens to pull our dollar down toward the 70-cent level. Per capita, Canada is among the richest countries in raw materials. There is no question that our economy depends more on raw materials than do those of most other countries. However, the depressed economic situation has caused a slump in prices of many of the commodities we sell abroad. Grain, copper, nickel, and lumber are going at give-away prices. There is no question that years of high living by all governments beyond their means, and intrusions and interference into the free enterprise system on a scale that Canada simply cannot afford are now exacting their toll. They only aggravate the impact of weak commodity prices; no wonder "short sellers", sellers of the Canadian dollar, have a constant field day.
As I mentioned earlier, although this budget has totally failed to address itself to the underlying causes of our problems, it has offered some band-aid remedies which may bring forth some short-term assistance to a few taxpayers, to a few prospective home buyers and to a few farmers and businesses.
1 refer to the proposal to subsidize interest rates for farmers over the next two years to 4 per cent below the 16.5 per cent currently offered through the Farm Credit Corporation. Although it may be a case of too litttle too late, it is a start, and for that reason it is welcome. Offering a $3,000 grant to

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
first-time home owners and new home buyers also merits some support. One drawback is that the program is effective only until December 31 of this year. 1 believe that to help stimulate the housing industry the program should be extended. I hope that this proposal will nevertheless stimulate demand for new homes so that more jobs to build those homes will be created.
Also welcome is the $750 million that has been earmarked for direct job creation. Reducing interest rates by 4 per cent to small businesses is welcome news. The Small Business Development Bond in a new form will, I hope, help out this depressed sector of the economy to a certain extent. It goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that this aid to farmers, to small businesses, and to home owners should be put into effect as soon as possible. There should be no more delays like the kind we saw over the last seven months since the November budget. Delays only result in more uncertainty, more bankruptcies, more businesses going belly up and more farmers losing their farms and livelihood, so I urge the government to make all haste in getting their programs in place as soon as possible.
The unfortunate part of these programs is that only a small percentage of Canadians, a handful-those who are in desperate need of assistance-will benefit from these programs. The rest will be left to their fate, to sink or swim, caught in this terrible situation through no fault of their own, brought on by forces over which they had no control, and now they have to suffer because of the mistakes of others. They have to suffer because of economic judgment from those advisers who should have known better, governments, the banking community and others whose advice and guidance proved totally wrong and totally inaccurate.
There is no justice when people have to suffer because of the gross mistakes of others. As I have mentioned, the government has borrowed a tremendous amount of money over the last ten years or so. We have seen an unlimited growth in the size of government and in the size of the government payroll. If the federal government does not wind down its own size and get its own house in order, if it does not curb borrowing and leave more disposable income in private hands for investment purposes then, Mr. Speaker, I am very much afraid that this government will be heading for total disaster, dragging all Canadians down with it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this chance to rise to speak and to offer my full support to a very good budget. It is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate tonight because some very notable speeches have been made over the last six days by members from all parties. I would like to extend my congratulations and thanks particularly to my colleagues who have been so helpful in the debate over the last few days.
I believe this is a budget which attacks the worst economic ills that we are currently experiencing in our economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You made them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a budget which attacks inflation, the basis of it all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It reminds us that a 6 per cent world will restore our strength, but the 12 per cent world we are currently experiencing will continue to sap that strength.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who created it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a budget which attacks unemployment, the worst and most direct punishment that we experience from inflation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You caused it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This budget offers $500 million right away for short-term job creation. This is a budget that offers interest rate relief.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How does it reduce inflation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is a budget which offers almost $900 million for housing, for small business and for farms for shortterm interest rate relief.
This is a budget which offers a long-term answer to the horrors and the continued effects of high interest rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a hoax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a bold new tax proposal in this budget that will help both the lender and the borrower to enjoy security and some reasonable level of interest on his borrowings.
This budget attacks the most basic economic ills that we are currently experiencing. I believe that this is a budget which has been well received across our country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: People need the 6 per cent target that we have offered them, and they welcome getting it from us. They welcome this leadership.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What leadership?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: People need the new jobs that were created and they welcome the new spending that we have directed into job creation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They welcome the $20 billion deficit?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
People need the interest rate relief now. They support the grants that we are extending to business, to housing and to farmers. People need the long-term hopes that we are extending to our new tax incentives.
Let us take a look at what some of the people have said about the budget since we issued it a week ago. Let us go to
July 8. 1982

the newspapers. For example, the Citizen on June 29 had an article which reads in part:
John Bulloch, head of the 68,000-member Canadian Federation of Independent Business and outspoken critic of the ill-fated November budget, said Finance Minister Allan MacEachen "deserves full marks" for attempting to restrain federal public service wages.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did he say on the thirtieth?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The article continues:
John Kyle, chairman of the economic policy committee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce ... applauded the "signal to the rest of us" contained in the measures designed to hold the line on federal public service wages.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then what did he say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The same article continued:
But Alasdair McKichan, president of the Retail Council of Canada, said he expected Finance Minister Allan MacEachen's proposals to have an immediate beneficial effect on the level of employment and the Canadian dollar.
"It may also be the turning point in the breaking of the inflation psychology," he said. "My first reaction is that it was a pretty intelligent approach to a very difficult situation. He should get marks for ingenuity."
McKichan said he was particularly impressed by the proposals to partially abandon indexation of benefits.
"This showed the public sector they weren't the only ones getting hit."
Let me turn to the Canadian Press of June 29, as well, to see some of the comments which people have made. Jim Webber, deputy chief economist of the Toronto-Dominion Bank agreed by saying, "MacEachen has made all the right sort of moves". In the same report, Lloyd McGinnis, president of the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce, said that the imposition of wage restraints on the public sector showed good leadership. He said that the move will provide a realistic position for wage negotiations in the private sector. This is an important piece of information.
Now I should like to turn to what Jack McArthur had to say in The Toronto Star on June 29. He said:
MacEachen is dead right about this: Inflation is the Number One enemy. Not so much because it means that prices rise for consumers as because:
Fast-rising prices result in high interest rates, which kill both economic growth and the new investment that creates it.
Further on in the same article he said:
Fast-inflating costs make us less competitive with producers in nations where costs are going up more slowly.
Also in the same article he said:
Short-term job creation-as promised by the finance minister-is meaningless unless the prices of the goods produced by the workers become attractive in the long run.
This reality is recognized in the MacEachen budget.
He went on to say:
MacEachen's objective of 6 per cent or less in annual inflation is right on.
He concluded the article by noting:
In the end, inflation will write the story. If it can be brought down, other good things will follow. If it can't, even a budget a month won't help.
There are other people across the country who have had things to say about the budget, and I should like to quote them. Turning to the Telegraph Journal of June 30, an article
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
appeared entitled, "Saint John Budget Reaction-Labour Official 'Sickened'; Businessmen 'Optimistic'". In part it read:
Patrick Darrah, president of the Saint John Construction Association ... and Keith Bowman, a tax consultant with Clarkson Gordon, both said they were gratified to see that the government is setting up an advisory board to consult on a number of economic proposals put forth last night. They said it was a sign the government is listening to what people are saying.
According to the articles, Mr. Bowman said:
Mr. MacEachen "did pretty well almost as much as he could do" considering the confines in which he was working. He said the public sector wage restraint program was good, but would need to filter over into the private sector-
Ronald Anderson wrote in The Globe and Mail under the heading, "Indexed loan plan is urgently needed" about our attack on interest rates. He said:
-Finance Minister Allan MacEachen has put forward one proposal that cuts to the heart of Canada's economic problems.
The single overriding constraint that is throttling the economy is the extraordinarily high level of interest rates.
The answer to this problem is, not to abandon the fight against inflation, and not for Ottawa to seal off the borders to keep money in the country while it orders a reduction in Canadian interest rates. But a practical and rational approach to the issue of high interest rates is offered by Mr. MacEachen's proposal for a system of new financing instruments that would be indexed to the rate of inflation.
He went on to note:
The important point to be noted is that the rising monthly payments under a fully indexed plan would not become more onerous if the borrower's income rises at the rate of inflation.
Finally at the end of the article he said:
The five or six percentage point relief that would come from exempting the illusionary inflation component of interest from taxation might, when it reaches the borrower, be just enough to save some major corporations from bankruptcy.
My last quotation is from The Gazette of Montreal dated June 29, 1982 under the heading, "Housing spokesmen see hope in MacEachen's grants plans". It reads:
The combination of measures in last night's federal budget looked "positive" for the future of the depressed housing industry, says John Sandusky, vicepresident of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada.
The article continued:
But he said a whole package of measures means "we've got a pretty good shot at renewed activity in our business."
Further on it indicated:
According to MacEachen, all home owners having to spend more than 30 per cent of their gross income as a result of renewals taking place from now on will be eligible for a grant of up to $3,000.
Sandusky said the grant will ease the worry for many home owners whose mortgages come up for renewal soon.
A final comment in the article read:
An official of the Quebec Provincial Home Builders Association predicted "things will move very fast" in the industry following MacEachen's announcement of grants to home buyers.
I think this is a very positive and a very representative sampling of reactions to the budget which we announced a week ago.
Now I should like to take a look at some of the details. Earlier I said that the budget sets out as its basis an attack on inflation. We regard inflation, as we have said regularly to

July 8, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
Canadian people, as the basic disease from which our economy is suffering. We have gone after that by providing for Canadian people a measure of leadership by restraining government wage costs to the 6 per cent and the 5 per cent indexing levels. In addition, we have asked Canadians to join in this effort by restraining indexing growth on some of our major costs and some of our programs. Then we can reallocate the funds from those programs into the stimulation of our economy so that other Canadians can have jobs and have relief from the heavy burden of interest rates on their businesses, farms and fishing efforts.
The major stimulation in the second part of the budget is a short-term piece of relief for those people most deeply hit by the impact of inflation, high interest rates and unemployment. Let me look at the way we have reallocated money inside our savings. We put $100 million into farming programs through the Farm Credit Corporation. Small businesses are getting $400 million through the small business investment grant, money which they can use to buy new equipment for research and development and for the all-important expansion we need to get our economy going again.
The housing package is one of the most exciting. Earlier I read a few comments from spokesmen in the housing industry. The renovation plan which was announced a few months ago has been so successful that we have found room to expand it and to double our contribution. We have given more flexibility and more leeway in the Canadian rental supply program so that developers can get involved and build the units which we consider so vital to take pressure off the rental housing market. Current home owners who are suffering under the difficulty of high mortgage costs can now obtain direct grants of $3,000.
Under the Canada mortgage renewal plan, people who spend more than 30 per cent of their gross family income can get the cost of their mortgages written down to a more intelligent and more bearable level. For new home buyers, for people coming into the home buying market in the first place, we are able to give an additional $3,000 grant to write down the cost of interest rates to encourage these people to come out into housing markets. First-time buyers are encouraged to buy older or new homes. Current home owners are asked to go out and buy new homes altogether. This gives us the double benefit of giving relief to Canadians who need the relief and of creating jobs for people who need the jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One member opposite expresses his admiration for high levels of employment by saying that any job-creation program is nonsense, obviously his high regard for any effort to take pressure off people who need some help.
The final proposal we are attempting to implement along this line is to throw another $3 million into our job-creation program and $200 million into direct job-creation programs.
All of this-$1.5 billion of expenditures-is short-term relief for our economy.
We do not pretend that this figure, massive though it is, is a permanent relief for the economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us go to the polls.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We offer this relief to help Canadians who need that help now. These programs are now available. People can get the application forms. Businesses can receive the money and begin again now. This money is circulated inside the current level of government spending. This is how we have tried to take the sharing about which my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) spoke so eloquently a few moments ago by asking people to share through giving small amounts themselves to create a large amount which we can use for those people who are most in need.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is nothing left to share.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) says that there is nothing left to share. I would think that $1.5 billion is a lot of money to share. It is a small amount from each individual but it is a large pot.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One big deficit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The jobs which will be created will indeed be welcomed by the people who obtain them. Small businesses will welcome the grants they receive. The housing which will be created will be welcomed by the people who get it. Farmers who receive relief from interest rates will welcome that. These are measures which the hon. member for Edmonton North believes are not welcomed. He thinks they are indeed insignificant. Perhaps he should go out to the country to talk to some of those people who will benefit.
Once this short-term relief is finished this budget makes a proposal which will help businessmen to index their capital gains in order to stimulate investment in Canadian companies. We see in this budget an exciting new plan which will offer lower interest rates at first to people with mortgages, at first to farmers-

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No one can make the payments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a plan that will allow people to lend their money with a great deal of security knowing that they will get a safe return. It will equally give security to those people who need to borrow money. It will help people who need to know how much interest rates will be for the next few years in order to make their long-term plans. They will be able to take advantage of this new proposal in the white paper. That proposal has been very well received indeed by the business community.
What is equally important is that the proposal has been put out for consultation to the business community, a process that has been welcomed in itself. The proposal of a major tax change has been submitted to the business community for the first time for its detailed study and scrutiny so that it may have public imput and allow the public to have a part to play in forming future tax policy. I believe this speaks well of the
July 8, 1982

government and of the deep concern that we have for reform in the tax process as announced in the minister's green paper.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are stealing that from Bob Stanfield. Be honest!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us review what some of our hon. friends in the House have had to say about the budget in the last six days.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We can hear the enthusiasm they have expressed for it. In my judgment, the debate has taken a strange and false turn. I think it is time for some of us to come back to earth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us look for a moment at the position taken by our friends on the left.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no one further to the left than you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To my thinking they represent the all or nothing school of thought. Nothing could have illustrated that philosophy more clearly than the position taken by that party yesterday when they were given an opportunity to extend real relief on the UFFI problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Louder!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They stonewalled. Why did they do that? Because they said that relief was not enough. It was either an all or nothing proposition. If they did not get their way, no home owner or anyone suffering would get any relief. It was not enough, so no one would get help.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us go to the people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the situation with this budget as well. They are predicting failure and thereby encouraging everyone to continue this game of all or nothing. They are saying over and over again that no one needs to take 6 per cent because the government will fail.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because the government has forced it down their throats.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This may be a great bargaining tool during prosperous times. Let us remember, however, that when times are tough and the game is all or nothing, the answer is far too often "nothing".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell that to the oil companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The pie today is too small. It is neither compassionate nor sensitive to urge people to take more and more when the real answer will be less and less until it becomes nothing.
With the UFFI issue yesterday, they demonstrated the falsehood of their argument.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
The Budget-Mr. Fisher

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They said they will take nothing unless they have it their way, and they are saying the same thing today when they talk about wage levels and the fight against inflation. They are urging people to go for the moon-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We want you to go to the moon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-but instead people are going broke. I would welcome the kind of sanity and good judgment that was reflected by a union leader who is currently under great stress. The president of Inco workers, local 6500 Ron MacDonald who urged rejection of the earlier offer, reluctantly recommended acceptance of the new pact. Why? The answer is in The Globe and Mail issue of July 5, if members want to look it up. It reads:
'But after the company announced a four-month production shutdown on June 23, I had to start thinking we weren't hurting them, that maybe it was better to pick another time and another place to take the company on.
That man expressed very clearly and practically that you cannot always go for all or nothing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not feel that way. We will take you on any time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That reality is forcing itself on us. I thank that union leader for being much more realistic than my hon. friends here.
This government is not saying all or nothing. We are saying that everyone is in this together. We are saying that from the lowest to the highest pay scale, from the youngest to the oldest, companies and unions, the public sector and private sector, whether it is wages or prices, we are all in this together and we must break the 12 per cent cycle and restore health to our economy.
As a last warning to my all or nothing friends, I am reminded of an example I saw in the Caribbean during the winter where I visited a small country with limited resources. I was at a forestry station which the Canadian government was supporting. I was told that the forestry station was an utter failure that year. I asked why and was told that they were unable to bring the crops in. When I asked why this occurred, I was told that the previous government of just a few months earlier had given their workers a 100 per cent pay raise out of a deep sense of compassion. The government had run out of money and fired half of the workers. That is not compassion, it is not practical but it is a very good example of what happens when you ask for too much from a limited pie. Not only do the workers lose, the whole economy fails. The management and the whole country fails.
Let us now consider the position of the hon. members across from us. If the NDP are offering "all or nothing", then the Conservatives are offering us "divide and conquer". Again, they do it in the name of compassion. Again, they do it by error. One by one, they drag out the groups. One by one, they
